text: 1.1. King Tarquinius, having proved the author of no small nor few benefits to the Romans, after holding the sovereignty thirty-eight years thus died, leaving two grandsons who were still infants and two daughters already married to men. His successor in the rule was his son-in-law Tullius, in the fourth year of the fiftieth Olympiad, the one in which Epitelides the Laconian won the foot-race, Archestratides being archon at Athens. It is now the proper time to relate the things I passed over at the outset concerning him: from what parents he was sprung, and what deeds he performed while still a private citizen and before he came to the sovereignty.

1.2. The account given of his lineage, the one to which I myself most of all subscribe, is as follows. In Corniculum, a city of the Latin nation, a certain man of the royal family, Tullius by name, was wedded to Ocrisia, the fairest and most virtuous of the women in Corniculum. When the city was taken by the Romans, this Tullius was slain fighting, and Ocrisia, who was with child, was chosen out of the spoils by King Tarquinius and given as a gift to his own wife. She, learning everything concerning the woman, not long afterwards set her free, and continued to cherish and honour her above all women.

1.3. From this Ocrisia, while she was still a slave, a child was born, to whom, when he had been reared, his mother gave the proper and family name Tullius, after his father, but the common and appellative name Servius, after her own fortune, because she had borne him while in servitude. Servius, if rendered into the Greek tongue, would be Doulios.

2.1. There is also another account preserved in the local records concerning his birth, one that exalts the circumstances of his life into the realm of the marvellous, which I have found in many Roman histories — if indeed such a tale is acceptable to gods and divinities. It tells that from the hearth of the palace, on which the Romans perform other sacred rites and consecrate the first portions of their meals, there rose up above the fire the privy member of a man; and that Ocrisia was the first to behold it, as she was carrying the customary cakes to the fire, and that she at once went and told the king and queen.

2.2. Tarquinius, on hearing it and afterwards seeing the prodigy, was filled with wonder; but Tanaquil, who besides her general wisdom was inferior to none of the Tyrrhenians in her knowledge of divination, told him that it was fated for an offspring greater than mortal nature to spring from the royal hearth out of the woman who should be united with the apparition. And when the other interpreters of prodigies declared the same, the king resolved that Ocrisia, to whom the prodigy had first appeared, should be united with it; and thereupon the woman, adorned as brides are wont to be adorned, was shut up alone in the room in which the prodigy had been seen.

2.3. One of the gods or lesser divinities, then, having lain with her and afterwards vanished — whether it was Vulcan, as some suppose, or the tutelary hero of the house — she conceived and bore Tullius at the appointed time. This tale, which does not seem altogether worthy of belief, is rendered less incredible by another divine manifestation, marvellous and astonishing, that occurred concerning the man.

2.4. For once, when he was lying in the colonnade of the palace asleep about midday, a fire shone out about his head; and his mother and the king's wife, as they were passing through the colonnade, beheld it, as did all who chanced to be present with the women at the time; and the flame continued to play about his whole head until his mother ran up and roused him, whereupon the flame, dispersed together with his sleep, vanished away. Such, then, are the accounts given concerning his birth.

3.1. The deeds worthy of record which he performed before becoming king — those by which Tarquinius came to admire him and the Roman people deemed him worthy of the honour next to the king — were as follows. While still a stripling he was enrolled among the cavalry in the first campaign which Tarquinius made against the Tyrrhenians, and he was thought to have fought so well that he immediately became famous and was the first of all to receive the prize for valour. Then, when another expedition was made against the same nation and a hard-fought battle took place near the city of Eretum, he showed himself the bravest of all and was again honoured by the king with crowns for valour.

3.2. When he was about twenty years of age he was appointed commander of the auxiliary force which the Latins sent, and he helped King Tarquinius to gain the dominion of the Tyrrhenians. In the first war against the Sabines also, being appointed commander of the horse, he routed the enemy's cavalry, and pursuing them as far as the city of Antemnae, won the prize for valour from that battle as well; and in many other battles which he fought against the same nation, sometimes leading the horse and sometimes the foot, he showed himself in all of them the bravest in spirit and was crowned before the rest.

3.3. And when that nation came to the point of submitting to the Romans and surrendering their cities, he was thought to have been the chief cause of this acquisition to Tarquinius and was crowned by him with the crowns of victory. He was, moreover, most sagacious in matters of statecraft, inferior to none in setting forth in speech the things resolved upon, and most able to accommodate himself to every fortune and to assimilate himself to every kind of person.

3.4. For these reasons the Romans saw fit to transfer him from the plebeians to the patricians by their vote, as they had earlier done with Tarquinius and, before him, with Numa Pompilius; and the king made him his kinsman by betrothing to him one of his daughters, and entrusted to him the performance of all those things which through sickness or old age he himself was unable to carry out, committing to his charge not only his own household but also the public affairs of the city. In all of these he was found faithful and just, and the commons thought it made no difference whether Tarquinius or Tullius had charge of the public business: so thoroughly had he won them over by his benefactions.

4.1. This man, then, having been endowed by nature with a character sufficiently equipped for command, and having received from Fortune many great occasions, when it came to pass that Tarquinius died, the victim of a plot by the sons of Ancus Marcius who wished to recover their father's sovereignty — as I have related in the preceding Book — and being thought to be summoned to the kingship by the very circumstances, he, being a man of action, did not let the opportunity slip from his hands.

4.2. She who helped him to establish his sovereignty and was the author of all his blessings was the wife of the deceased king, both because she was assisting her own son-in-law and because she knew from many oracles that it was fated for that man to reign over the Romans. It happened that a young son of hers had died not long before, leaving behind two infant children by him.

4.3. Reflecting upon the desolation of the house and being greatly afraid lest the Marcii, if they seized the rule, should destroy the children and blot out the whole royal kin, she first gave orders that the doors of the palace be shut and set guards over them with instructions to let no one pass either in or out. Then, ordering all the others to leave the chamber in which they had laid Tarquinius half-dead, and detaining only Ocrisia and Tullius and her daughter, who was wedded to Tullius, and ordering the children to be brought in by their nurses, she said to them:

4.4. "Our king Tarquinius, Tullius — he with whom you found nurture and education, and who honoured you above all his friends and kinsmen — having suffered impious treatment, has fulfilled his destiny without making any disposition concerning his private affairs or giving any charge concerning the public and political ones; indeed, he was not even able to greet any of us or to address us with his last farewells. These poor children are left desolate and orphaned, running no slight risk for their very lives. For if the affairs of the city fall to the Marcii who slew their grandfather, they will be destroyed by them in the most pitiable manner; nor will life be safe for you, to whom Tarquinius betrothed his daughters, slighting those men, if his murderers gain the rule; nor for his other friends and kinsmen, nor for us wretched women; but they will try to destroy us all, openly and by stealth.

4.5. Reflecting upon these things, then, we must not look on while these impious men who slew him, the enemies of us all, acquire so great a dominion; rather we must oppose and prevent them — for the present using craft and guile, for that is what the present moment requires; but when our first measures have prospered according to our purpose, then meeting them openly with all our force and with arms, if indeed there be need of that too. But there will be no need, if we are willing now to do what must be done.

4.6. And what is this? First, let us conceal the death of the king and contrive that it be given out to all that he has received no mortal wound, and let the physicians say that they will show him recovered within a few days. Then I will come forth into public view and tell the multitude that Tarquinius has charged me to say this: that, until he himself recovers from his wounds, he appoints as overseer and guardian of all things, both private and public, one of his sons-in-law — naming you, Tullius. And this will not be against the Romans' will; rather they will desire that the city be administered by you, by whom

4.7. it has often already been administered before. And when we have dispelled the present danger — for none of our enemies is any longer strong, so long as the king is reported to live — do you, taking the rods and the authority over arms, summon before the people those who plotted to slay Tarquinius, beginning with the sons of Marcius, and bring them to trial. After punishing all these — with death, if they submit to the trials; with perpetual exile and confiscation of their property, if they leave the cases undefended, which I think they are the more likely to do — set in order the affairs of the rule, winning over the multitude by humane intercourse, taking great care that no act of injustice be committed, and drawing to yourself the poorer citizens by certain benefits and gifts. Then, when it seems to us the right moment, let us announce that

4.8. Tarquinius is dead and conduct his funeral openly. It is your duty, Tullius — you who were reared by us and educated and have shared in all the good things which sons receive from a mother and father, and who are wedded to our daughter — if indeed you are to become king of the Romans, with me too contending at your side toward this end, to show a father's goodwill toward these children; and when they come to manhood and become capable of conducting public affairs, to declare the elder of them ruler of the Romans."

5.1. Having said this and having cast each of the children into the arms of her son-in-law and her daughter, and having stirred up much pity in both, when the moment came she went out of the chamber and ordered those within to make ready the things needful for the treatment and to call together the physicians. Then, letting the intervening night pass, on the following day, when a great crowd had run together to the palace, she came forth into public view, taking her stand at the windows that looked out upon the lane before the doors. First she pointed out to those present the men who had plotted the murder against the king, and brought forward in chains those who had been sent by

5.2. them to do the deed. Then, when she saw that many were lamenting the calamity and were filled with hatred of the perpetrators, she ended by telling them that nothing had come of the impious designs of the men, since they had not been able to kill Tarquinius. And when all received the news with gladness, she then commended Tullius to them as one appointed by the king to be overseer of all things, both private and public, until he himself should recover.

5.3. The people, then, departed full of joy that the king had suffered no terrible harm, and for a long time they continued to hold this belief. Tullius, having a strong band about him and bringing with him the royal lictors, came forth into the Forum and made proclamation that the Marcii should appear to stand trial; and when they did not obey, he proclaimed perpetual exile against them and, confiscating their estates to the public treasury, now held the rule of Tarquinius in security.

6.1. But before going on with the narrative I wish to render the reasons why I have agreed neither with Fabius nor with the other historians who write that the children left behind by Tarquinius were his sons, lest any of those who have read those histories suppose that I am writing carelessly in calling the children not his sons but his grandsons. For the historians have published this account about them altogether without consideration and carelessly, having examined none of the impossibilities and absurdities that overthrow it; each of which I shall try to make clear in a few words.

6.2. Tarquinius removed from Tyrrhenia, breaking up his whole household, when he was at the prime of life for judgment; for it is recorded that he was already claiming the right to take part in public life, to hold office, and to manage the common affairs, and that he made his departure thence because he had no share in any honour in the city.

6.3. Now another might suppose that he was at least in his thirtieth year when he departed from Tyrrhenia, since it is from this age that the laws for the most part summon those who wish to hold office and to manage public affairs; but I assume him to have been five whole years younger still, and make him to have departed in his twenty-fifth year. And indeed that he brought with him a Tyrrhenian wife, whom he had married while his father was still living, is agreed by all who have written the Roman histories.

6.4. He arrived at Rome in the reign of Ancus Marcius — according to Gellius, in the first year of that reign; according to Licinius, in the eighth. Let it be granted, then, that he came in the year in which Licinius writes, and not earlier; for he could not have come at a later time, since indeed in the ninth year of the rule of Ancus he was sent by the king, as commander of the horse, to the war against the Latins, as both these historians say. If, then, he came to Rome being no more than twenty-five years of age, and having become a friend of King Ancus in the eighth year of his reign, spent the remaining seventeen years with him — for Ancus reigned twenty-four years — and if he himself held the kingship thirty-eight years, as all agree, he would have been eighty years old when he died. For from the reckoning

6.5. of the years this total is gathered. And the wife, if she was five years younger than he, as is likely, would have been in her seventy-fifth year when Tarquinius died. If, then, she bore the younger of the sons last when she was in her fiftieth year — for beyond this time a woman no longer conceives, but this is the very limit of childbearing, as those who have examined these matters write — this son would have been not less than twenty-five years old at his father's death, and the elder, Lucius, not less than twenty-seven. It is not, therefore, the case that Tarquinius

6.6. left behind infant sons born of this woman. But if indeed the children were of manhood's age when their father died, neither would their mother have been so wretched and god-stricken as to deprive her own children of the rule which their father left them and to bestow it as a favour upon a stranger born of a slave-woman; nor would the children themselves, robbed of their father's rule, have borne the injustice in slack and careless fashion, and that at the very prime of their power to speak and to act. For Tullius did not surpass them in nobility of birth, being the son of a slave mother, nor did he differ greatly in the dignity of age, being older than one of them by only three years; so that they would not willingly have yielded the kingship to him.

7.1. The matter has also certain other absurdities, of which all who have composed Roman histories were ignorant save one, whose name I shall mention shortly. For it is agreed that, after the death of Tarquinius, Tullius received the kingship and held it forty-four years; so that, if the elder of the Tarquinii was twenty-six years old at the time when he was deprived of the rule, he would have been over seventy when he killed Tullius.

7.2. But the historians have recorded that he was at the prime of his strength at that time, and they say that he himself lifted up Tullius from the senate-house and, carrying him outside, hurled him down the steps. His own expulsion from the rule takes place in the twenty-fifth year after that, and in that year he is introduced as campaigning in the war against the Ardeates and performing all the operations in person; but there is no reason in his being mustered for wars at the age of ninety-six.

7.3. And after being driven from the rule, he is said to have made war on the Romans for not less than fourteen years, taking part in affairs himself, as they say — which is contrary to the common opinions of all men — and the term of his life appears to be more than a hundred and ten years; but our regions do not produce such length of life.

7.4. Some of the Roman historians, aware of these absurdities, have tried to resolve them by other absurdities, making the mother of the children not Tanaquil but a certain Gegania, concerning whom we have received no account. Thus Tarquinius's marriage again becomes ill-timed, since he was little short of eighty years old; and the begetting of children is incredible for men of that age; nor was he childless, so as to desire offspring at all costs, but he had two daughters, and these

7.5. already married. Reckoning up each of these impossibilities and absurdities, then, I write that the children were not the sons of Tarquinius but his grandsons, agreeing with Lucius Piso the Frugi; for he alone has recorded these things in his Annals — unless indeed the children were by birth the king's grandsons, but his sons by adoption, and this was the cause of the error to all the others who have written the Roman histories. These things having been stated beforehand, it is now time to return to the remaining narrative.

8.1. When Tullius, having taken over the guardianship of the kingdom and having driven out the faction of the Marcii, now believed that he securely held the rule, he honoured the king Tarquinius — as one but lately dead of his wounds — with a costly funeral, the construction of a notable tomb, and the other honours; and for the time thereafter, as guardian of the children of the royal line, he made both their private welfare and the public affairs of the city the object of his watchfulness and care.

8.2. But what was being done was not to the liking of the patricians; rather they were indignant and bore it ill, not thinking it right that he should contrive for himself a kind of royal authority, when neither the senate had voted it nor the other things prescribed by law had been carried out. So the most powerful among them, meeting together often, conferred with one another about overthrowing this unlawful rule, and they resolved that, as soon as they should be convened in the senate by Tullius, they would compel the man to lay down the rods and the rest of the insignia of office; and when this should be done, to appoint the so-called interreges and through them to choose, according to the laws, the one who should rule the

8.3. city. While they were planning this, Tullius, getting wind of it, turned to courting the favour of the people and to cultivating the poorer citizens, hoping through them to retain the rule; and having summoned the multitude to an assembly, he brought the children forward upon the platform and delivered a speech of the following kind.

9.1. "Great necessity has come upon me, fellow citizens, to care for these children, who are infants. For Tarquinius, their grandfather, taking me up when I was fatherless and without a city, reared me as in no way inferior to his own children, and gave me one of his daughters to wife; and throughout all the time of his life he continued to honour and love me, as you also know, as though I had been born of himself; and when the matter of the conspiracy befell him, he entrusted to me, in case he should suffer anything human,

9.2. the care of the children. Who, then, will reckon me holy toward the gods or just toward men, if I forsake and betray the orphans, to whom I owe so many favours? But I will not betray my own faith nor forsake the children's desolation, so far as lies in my power. And it is just that you too should remember the benefits which their grandfather conferred upon the commonwealth, in subjecting to you so many cities of the Latins that disputed the rule, in making subject to you all the Tyrrhenians, the most powerful of your neighbours, and in compelling the Sabine nation to come under your hand — accomplishing all this amid many and great dangers.

9.3. So long, then, as he himself lived, it was fitting that you should acknowledge to him your gratitude for these benefits; but now that he has ended his life, it is fitting to render the recompense to his descendants, and not to bury, together with the bodies of your benefactors, the memory of their deeds as well. Consider yourselves, therefore, all jointly left as guardians of the children, and confirm to them the rule which their grandfather left. For they would not derive so great a benefit from my single protection as from the common aid of you all.

9.4. I have been compelled to say this because I perceive that certain men are combining against them and wish to hand over the rule to others. And I ask you, men of Rome, remembering my own struggles which I waged on behalf of the sovereignty — struggles neither small nor few, which I need not recount to you who know them — to render to these children the gratitude owed to me in return for them. For I have chosen to manage the public affairs, not to procure a private rule for myself — of which I should have been worthy as much as any man, had I wished to obtain it — but to aid the family of Tarquinius.

9.5. And I become a suppliant of you, that you not forsake the orphans, who now run a danger concerning the rule, and who, if the first attempt of their enemies prospers according to plan, will also be driven from the city. But concerning these matters, as you have recognized what is needful and will do all that is fitting, I need say no more. But hear from me the benefits which I myself am prepared to confer upon you, and for the sake of which I have summoned the assembly.

9.6. As many of you as, being already in debt, are unable through poverty to pay — being eager to help these men, since they are citizens and have endured many toils on behalf of their country, that those who secured the common liberty may not be deprived of their own — from my own

9.7. funds I give you the means to discharge your debts. And as many as shall borrow hereafter, these I will not allow to be led off in bondage for their debts, and I will enact a law that no one shall lend on the security of free persons, deeming it sufficient for the creditors to have control of the property of those who have contracted with them. And that you may henceforth bear more lightly the contributions made to the public treasury, on account of which the poor are burdened and compelled to contract loans, I will order all to have their properties assessed and each to contribute from the assessment the amount that falls to him, as I learn is done in the greatest and best-governed cities; for I deem it both just and advantageous to the commonwealth that those who possess much should contribute much, and those who have little, little.

9.8. It seems to me, moreover, that of the public land, which you possess, having acquired it by arms, the most shameless should not, as now, hold it — men who have neither received it as a favour nor acquired it by purchase — but rather those of you who have no allotment, that you may not be hired labourers, though free, nor till the possessions of others, but your own; for no noble spirit can arise in men who are in want of the daily necessities.

9.9. Above all these things, I have resolved to make the constitution equal and common, and justice the same for all toward all. For some have come to such a pitch of insolence that they think fit to outrage the common people and not even to regard the poor among you as free. That the greater and the lesser may both receive and render justice on equal terms, I will enact laws that prevent violence and guard justice; and I myself will at no time relax in providing for the equality of speech of all."

10.1. While he was speaking thus, much praise arose from the assembly: some praised him because he was faithful and just toward his benefactors; others because he was humane and magnanimous toward the poor; others because he was moderate and democratic toward the humbler sort; and all loved and admired him because he was a lawful and just

10.2. ruler. When the assembly had been dismissed, on the following days he ordered the debtors who were unable to keep their faith to register to whom they owed and how much each; and when he had received the registers, setting up tables in the Forum, he counted out the debts to the creditors in the sight of all.

10.3. Having accomplished this, he set forth in public a royal edict, that those who were enjoying the use of the public land and holding it privately should withdraw from it within a fixed time, and that those citizens who had no allotment should register with him. He also drew up laws, some renewing the ancient and neglected ones which Romulus and Numa Pompilius had introduced, others

10.4. establishing himself. While he was thus engaged in statecraft, the patricians bore it ill, seeing the power of the senate being dissolved, and they no longer took the same counsels, but ones opposite to their former ones.

10.5. For in the beginning they had set out to take away his unlawful rule by appointing interreges and through them choosing one who should hold the office according to the laws; but then they thought they ought to be content with the present state of things and to meddle no further. For the reflection came to them that, if the senate brought to power the man whom it preferred, the people would oppose it by taking up the vote; but if they should make the choice of the king depend on the people, all the curiae would vote for Tullius, and it would result that the man would seem to rule according to the laws. They concluded, therefore, that it was better for the man to hold the rule by stealing it and circumventing the citizens than by persuading them and openly receiving it.

10.6. But none of their calculations availed them: so completely did Tullius out-general them and hold the kingship against their will. For having for a long time contrived that reports should circulate through the city that the patricians were plotting against him, he came forth into the Forum clad in soiled raiment and downcast, accompanied by his mother Ocrisia, by Tanaquil the wife of Tarquinius, and by the whole royal kindred. And when a great crowd had run together at the strangeness of the sight, he summoned an assembly, came forward upon the platform, and delivered a speech somewhat as follows.

11.1. "No longer is my danger only on behalf of the children of Tarquinius, that they suffer no terrible thing from their enemies; but now fear for my own life also enters in, lest I receive bitter recompense for my justice. For I am being plotted against by the patricians, and certain of them have been denounced to me as conspiring to kill me — having no injustice, neither greater nor less, to charge against me, but vexed and aggrieved at the good I have done the people and am prepared to do.

11.2. The creditors are angry because I did not permit the poor among you to be deprived of their liberty, led off by them for their debts; those who are embezzling and holding the public lands, because they are compelled to give up the land which you acquired with your blood, as though they were being robbed of an ancestral inheritance and not surrendering what belongs to others; those exempted from the war-contributions, because they will be compelled to have their lives assessed and to contribute from the assessments; and all in common, because they will be accustomed to live according to written laws, giving and receiving justice with you on equal terms, and will no longer abuse the poor like bought slaves, as they now do.

11.3. And these complaints they have brought together into a common cause and have resolved and sworn together to bring back the exiles and to restore the kingship to the sons of Marcius — those whom you, when they had slain Tarquinius your king, a good man and a lover of his city, and had wrought so great a pollution, and had abandoned their trials by default and assessed exile against themselves, voted to debar from fire and water. And, had not the information come to me speedily, they were about, bringing in a foreign force, while it was still night, to bring back the exiles into the city in great numbers.

11.4. What followed you all surely know, even if I do not say it: that the Marcii, with the patricians aiding them, having seized power without effort, were about first to seize me, the guardian of the kings and the one who carried out the trials against them; then to make away with these children and all the other kinsmen and friends of Tarquinius; and to reckon our wives and mothers and daughters and the whole female sex as captives — being men who have in their nature much of the bestial and

11.5. the tyrannical. If, then, this too is your wish, plebeians — to bring back murderers and proclaim them kings, and to drive out the children of your benefactors and rob them of the rule left them by their grandfather — we will be content with our fortune. But, by all the gods and divinities who watch over the life of men, all of us becoming suppliants of you, together with our wives and children, in return for the many benefits with which Tarquinius, the children's grandfather, continued to serve you, and in return for the many in which I myself, according to my power, have been useful to you, we ask you to grant us this one gift: to make plain your own resolve.

11.6. For if you have supposed that certain others are worthier than we to obtain this honour, the children will depart, leaving the city to you, and the rest of the kindred of Tarquinius; and I will take some nobler counsel concerning myself. For my life has already been lived sufficiently both for virtue and for good repute, and I would not, having been cheated of your goodwill — which I have chosen in preference to every good — think it worth my while to live shamefully among other men. Take, then, the rods, and give them, if you wish, to the patricians; I will not trouble you by my presence."

12.1. While he was saying this and was making as if to withdraw from the platform, there arose from all an immense outcry and entreaties mingled with tears, that he should remain and keep hold of affairs, fearing no one. Then certain men, set on for the purpose and posted about the Forum, cried out that they should make him king, and demanded that the curiae be summoned and called for a vote. And when these had begun, at once the whole people came round to the same purpose.

12.2. Perceiving this, Tullius no longer let the moment pass, but, saying that he owed them many thanks because they remembered his benefits, and promising to do still more good if they should declare him king, he appointed a day for the election, to which he ordered all those from the country also to be present.

12.3. When the people had assembled, calling the curiae one by one, he distributed the votes. And being adjudged worthy of the kingship by all the curiae, he then received the rule from the multitude of the commons, bidding a long farewell to the senate, which he did not see fit to have ratify the decisions of the people, as was its custom. Having come to the kingship in this manner, he became the author of many other measures of statecraft, and he waged a great war, worthy of record, against the Tyrrhenians. But I will first speak of his measures of statecraft.

13.1. Immediately upon receiving the rule he distributed the public land among those Romans who served for hire; then he confirmed by the curiae the laws relating to contracts and to wrongs; these were about fifty in number, of which I need make no mention at present.

13.2. To the city he added two hills, the one called the Viminal and the Esquiline, each of which has the size of a considerable city, and he distributed them among those Romans who had no homes, to build houses upon; there too he himself made his dwelling, in the strongest part of the Esquiline.

13.3. This king was the last to enlarge the circuit of the city, adding the two hills to the five, after taking the auspices as the law required and performing the other rites due to the gods. But the building of the city advanced no further, the divine power, as they say, not permitting it; and all the districts about the city that are inhabited, many and large though they be, are unfortified and without walls,

13.4. and very easily made subject to enemies who come against them. And if anyone, looking at these, should wish to estimate the size of Rome, he will be forced to wander and will have no sure mark by which to judge how far the city, still advancing, extends, and where it begins to be city no longer: so closely is the town interwoven with the country, and it presents to those who behold it the impression of a city stretched out to infinity.

13.5. But if one should wish to measure it by the wall — which is hard to find because of the dwellings that surround it on many sides, though it preserves in many places some traces of its ancient construction — by the circuit that encloses the town of the Athenians, the circuit of Rome would appear to him not much larger. But concerning the size and beauty of the city, as it was in my own time, there will be another occasion more suitable for the narrative.

14.1. Tullius, then, when he had enclosed the seven hills with one wall, divided the city into four parts and gave to the parts names from the hills — to one Palatine, to another Suburan, to the third Colline, and to the fourth of the parts Esquiline — and made the city to be of four tribes, whereas it had been of three before.

14.2. And he ordered the men dwelling in each of the four parts, like villagers, neither to take up another dwelling nor to be enrolled anywhere else; and the levies of soldiers and the collections of money for military and other needs which each man had to furnish to the commonwealth, he made no longer according to the three tribes by birth, as before, but according to the four local tribes appointed by himself; and he set commanders over each division, like phylarchs or village-chiefs, whom he ordered to know what house each man dwelt in.

14.3. Then he ordered that in all the lanes shrines should be built by the neighbours, little chapels to the heroes of the crossways, and he enacted that sacrifices be performed to them every year, each household bringing cakes; and for those who celebrated the rites of the neighbours at the crossway-shrines he appointed that not the free, but the slaves, should be present and join in the rites, as though the service of the bondsmen were pleasing to the heroes;

14.4. this festival the Romans continued to keep even in my own day, a few days after the Saturnalia, with great solemnity and at great expense, calling it the Compitalia from the lanes — for they call the lanes compiti — and they preserve the ancient custom in the rites, propitiating the heroes through their servants and removing from them every mark of slavery during those days, that the slaves, being softened by this humanity — which has in it something great and solemn — may become more agreeable toward their masters and may bear the grievous things of fortune less heavily.

15.1. He divided all the country also, as Fabius says, into twenty-six parts, which he too calls tribes, adding to them the four city tribes; but as Vennonius has recorded, into thirty-one, so that with those in the city the thirty-five tribes still existing in our time were made up. Cato, however, who is more trustworthy than both of these, says that there were thirty tribes in all under Tullius, and does not distinguish the number of the parts.

15.2. Tullius, then, having divided the land into however many parts, established places of refuge upon the hills that could afford much security to the farmers, calling them by Greek names, Pagi, to which all fled together from the fields whenever there should be an inroad of enemies, and most often they

15.3. passed the night there. There were officers over these too, whose business it was to know the names of the farmers belonging to the same pagus and the possessions on which their livelihood depended; and whenever there was need to call the countrymen to arms or to collect money-contributions man by man, these gathered the persons and exacted the money. And that the number of these men might not be hard to find, but easy to reckon and plain, he ordered them to set up altars of the gods who watched over and guarded the pagus, whom he appointed should be honoured with common sacrifices every year, all assembling together; and he established this also as one of the most honoured festivals, the so-called Paganalia; and he drew up laws concerning these rites, which the Romans still keep under guard.

15.4. And for this sacrifice and the assembly he ordered all the members of the same pagus to contribute per head a certain fixed coin, one sum for the men, another for the women, and another for those under age. From this, when it was counted up by those in charge of the rites, the number of the people became evident, according to their kinds and their ages.

15.5. And as Lucius Piso records in the first book of his Annals, wishing also to know the number of those dwelling in the city — of those being born and those dying and those being enrolled among the men — he appointed what coin those concerned should pay over for each: into the treasury of Eilithyia, whom the Romans call Juno Lucina, for those being born; into that of Venus, who is established in the grove and whom they call Libitina, for those dying; into that of Youth, for those beginning to be counted among the men. From these he was to learn each year both how many there were in all and which of them were of military age.

15.6. Having established these things, he ordered all the Romans to register and to assess their properties in money, taking the lawful oath that they had assessed them truly and to the best of their judgment, writing down of what fathers they were sprung, declaring the age they were of, naming their wives and children, and adding in what tribe of the city or pagus of the country each dwelt. For the one who did not assess himself he fixed as penalty the loss of his property, and that the man himself be scourged and sold; and for a long time this law remained in force among the Romans.

16.1. When all had been assessed, taking up the registers and ascertaining both their number and the size of their estates, he introduced the wisest of all political measures and one which was the cause of the greatest blessings to the Romans, as the results showed.

16.2. The measure was as follows. He took out one portion from all, of which the greatest assessment of property was not less than a hundred minae. These, arranging them into eighty centuries, he ordered to bear as arms Argolic shields, spears, bronze helmets, breastplates, greaves, and swords. Dividing them into two, he made forty centuries of the younger men, to whom he assigned the campaigns in the field, and forty of the older, who were to remain in the city, when the youth went out to war, and guard what was within the walls.

16.3. This was the first class; it held in war the position fighting in front of the whole phalanx. Then from those who remained he took out another portion, those whose assessment was within ten thousand drachmae but not less than seventy-five minae. Arranging these into twenty centuries, he ordered them to bear the same arms as the former, except that he took away their breastplates and, instead of round shields, gave them oblong shields. Dividing off from among these too those over forty-five years from those of military age, he made ten centuries of the younger, who were to fight before the city, and ten of the older, to whom he assigned the guarding of the walls. This was the second class; it was arrayed in

16.4. the battles behind the front-fighters. The third class he made from those remaining who had an assessment less than seven thousand five hundred drachmae but not less than fifty minae. Of these he diminished the armament not only by the breastplates,

16.5. as for the second, but also by the greaves. He arranged these too into twenty centuries and divided them in the same manner as the former by ages, assigning ten centuries to the younger and ten to the older. The position and station of these centuries in battle was behind those posted behind the front-fighters.

17.1. Again taking out from those remaining those who had property less than five thousand drachmae down to twenty-five minae, he made a fourth portion. These too he arranged into twenty centuries, and made ten of those in their prime and ten of those over age, as with the former. He ordered them to bear as arms oblong shields, swords, and spears, and to hold in battle the last position.

17.2. The fifth portion, those whose livelihood was within twenty-five minae down to twelve and a half minae, he arranged into thirty centuries. These too were divided by age: fifteen of the centuries held the older men, fifteen the younger. He ordered these to serve outside the ranks armed with javelins and

17.3. slings. Four centuries having no arms at all he ordered to accompany those bearing arms; of these four, two were of armourers and carpenters and the others who made the things useful for war, and two of trumpeters and horn-blowers and those who signalled with certain other instruments the calls of war. The artisans were attached to those holding the second assessment, divided by age, the one century following the older, the other the younger.

17.4. The trumpeters and horn-blowers were arranged with the fourth portion. Of these too there was one century of the older and one of the younger; and the captains, chosen from all as the most valiant in war, made their several centuries obedient to the commands given them.

18.1. This was the arrangement that filled out the infantry, both the army of the phalanx-soldiers and the light-armed. The body of horse he chose from those having the greatest assessment and distinguished in birth; he arranged them into eighteen centuries and attached them to the first eighty centuries of the phalanx-soldiers; these too had the most distinguished captains.

18.2. The remaining citizens, who had an assessment less than twelve and a half minae and were more numerous than the former, he arranged all into a single century and freed them from military service and made them exempt from every contribution. There were, then, six divisions, which the Romans call classes, naming them by a paronym from the Greek call; for what we, framing it as an imperative, utter as kalei ("call"), they pronounce cala, and the classes they anciently called caleses;

18.3. and the centuries which the divisions comprised were one hundred and ninety-three. The first division contained ninety-eight centuries together with the horse; the second, twenty-two together with the artisans; the third, twenty; the fourth again twenty-two together with the trumpeters and horn-blowers; the fifth, thirty; and that posted last of all, one century, that of the poor.

19.1. Using this arrangement, he made the levies of soldiers according to the division of the centuries, and the assessment of contributions according to the valuations of estates. For whenever he had need of ten thousand or, it might be, twenty thousand soldiers, dividing the number among the hundred and ninety-three centuries, he ordered each century to furnish the number that fell to it; and reckoning the expense for the provisioning of the troops and the other supplies of war that were to be furnished, how much would suffice, dividing it in the same way among the hundred and ninety-three centuries, he ordered all to contribute the sum falling to each from the assessment.

19.2. The result, then, was that those having the greatest estates, being fewer but divided into more centuries, served more campaigns, never resting, and contributed more money than the rest; while those possessing moderate or small means, being more numerous in fewer centuries, served seldom and by turns and paid small contributions; and those possessing less than the required amount were exempt from all burdens.

19.3. He did each of these things not without reason, but being persuaded that for all men the prizes of wars are their possessions, and that all toil hard for the guarding of these; he thought it right, therefore, that those who risked greater prizes should endure greater hardships both in their persons and their property, that those who risked lesser should be less burdened in both respects, and that those who feared for nothing should suffer no hardship, being released from contributions because of their poverty and from campaigns because of their freedom from contribution. For the Romans did not at that time receive military pay from the public treasury, but served at their own expense.

19.4. He thought, then, that those who had nothing from which to contribute should not contribute money, but, lacking the daily necessities, should be excused; nor that any, contributing nothing, should serve being paid from the moneys of others, like mercenaries.

20.1. Having in this way laid all the burden, both of dangers and of expenses, upon the rich, when he saw them indignant, by another means he soothed their discouragement and softened their anger by bestowing on them an advantage from which they were to become masters of the whole constitution, driving the poor away from public affairs; and in accomplishing this he escaped the notice of the commons. The advantage concerned the assemblies, in which the greatest matters were ratified by the people.

20.2. It has been stated by me before that the people, by the ancient laws, had control of the three greatest and most necessary matters: to appoint the magistracies, both those in the city and those in the field; to ratify some laws and abolish others; and to decide concerning a war being undertaken or concluded. The consideration and judgment of these matters it made by voting according to the curiae; and those possessing the least had a vote equal to those having the greatest estates; and the rich being few, as is natural, the poor prevailed in the votings, being far more numerous than they.

20.3. Tullius, perceiving this, transferred the power of the votes to the rich. For whenever it seemed good to him to appoint magistracies, or to decide about a law, or to declare war, he convened the centuriate assembly instead of the curiate. He called first to declare their opinion the centuries enrolled from the highest assessment, among which were the eighteen of the horse and the eighty of the foot.

20.4. These, being three more than the remaining centuries, if they were of one mind, prevailed over the others, and the decision was reached. But if all these did not come to the same purpose, then he called the twenty-two centuries from the second assessment. And the votes being divided then too, he called those from the third assessment; and fourth, those from the fourth assessment. And this he did until ninety-seven centuries should be of like vote. But if down to the fifth call

20.5. this did not chance to happen, but the opinions of the hundred and ninety-two centuries were split into equal parts, then he called the last century, in which was the multitude of citizens who were poor and for that reason exempt from all military service and contribution; and to whichever of the parts this century attached itself, that part gained the victory. But this was rare and not far from impossible. For the most part the decision was reached at the first call, and seldom did it advance to the fourth; the fifth call and the last were superfluous.

21.1. Having established this measure and given the rich so great an advantage, he escaped the notice of the people, as I said, having out-generalled them and driven the poor away from public affairs. For all supposed that they had an equal share in the constitution, since they were each asked their opinions man by man in their own centuries; but they were deceived because there was one vote for the whole century, whether it contained few citizens or very many; and because the centuries having the greatest assessment voted first — being more in number than the rest, but containing fewer men; and most of all because the poor, being many, had a single vote and were called last.

21.2. This having come to pass, it less occurred to the rich — who spent much and received no respite from the dangers of war — to feel burdened, since they had become masters of the greatest things and had taken all the power from those who did not act as they did; while the poor, who had the smallest share in political affairs, bore their diminution in these matters reasonably and gently, being released from contributions and campaigns; and the city had the same men both to deliberate about its needs and to share most of all in the dangers and to do what was needful.

21.3. This order of the constitution remained guarded by the Romans for many generations; but in our times it has been shifted and changed to the more democratic, forced by certain strong necessities — not that the centuries were abolished, but that the calling of them no longer preserved the ancient exactness, as I have learned, having often been present at their elections. But concerning these matters the present is not the fitting occasion for the discussion.

22.1. At that time, then, when Tullius had ordered the matter of the assessments, ordering all the citizens to assemble in the largest of the plains before the city bearing their arms, and having arrayed the horse by squadrons, the foot in phalanx, and those equipped with the light armament each in their own centuries, he performed a lustration of them with a bull, a ram, and a he-goat. Ordering these victims to be led three times around the army, he sacrificed to Mars, who possesses that plain.

22.2. By this lustration even down to my own times the Romans purify themselves after the completion of the assessments, through those holding the most sacred office, calling it a Lustrum. The total number of the Romans who assessed their lives at that time was, as is recorded in the censorial writings, eighty thousand lacking three hundred.

22.3. This king took no small forethought also for the increase of the body politic, perceiving a thing which all the kings before him had neglected. For they, by receiving strangers and giving them a share in the equal citizenship, deeming no birth or fortune of theirs unworthy, advanced the city to great population.

22.4. But Tullius permitted even the freed among the servants, if they did not wish to depart to their own cities, to share in the equal citizenship. For ordering these too, together with all the other free persons, to assess their properties, he enrolled them in the four city tribes, in which the freedman class, however great it be, continues to be ranked even to our times; and he granted them a share of all the public privileges of which the other plebeians partook.

23.1. When the patricians were vexed at the matter and bore it ill, summoning the multitude to an assembly he said that he marvelled, first, at those who were indignant, if they thought that the free differed from the slave in nature rather than in fortune; and second, if they tested the worthy of honours not by their characters and manners but by their chance fortunes, seeing how unstable and quick to change a thing prosperity is, and how it is not easy for anyone, not even of the very blessed, to say for how long a time it

23.2. will remain with him. He bade them consider how many cities, both barbarian and Greek, had already changed from slavery to freedom, and how many from freedom to slavery; and he condemned much folly in them, if, while granting freedom to the worthy among their servants, they begrudged them the citizenship. He counselled them, if they thought them wicked, not to make them free; but if

23.3. good, not to overlook them as aliens. He said they were doing an absurd and ignorant thing, in permitting all strangers to share in the city without distinguishing their fortunes — not inquiring busily whether any of them had become free from slaves — yet deeming those who had been slaves among themselves unworthy of this favour; and he said that those who supposed they surpassed others in good sense did not see even the things at their feet, the most common, which were plain even to the basest: namely, that the masters would have great care not to free men readily, as being about to bestow on chance persons the greatest of human goods; and that the slaves would have still greater eagerness to be good toward their masters, if they learned that, being judged worthy of freedom, they would forthwith be citizens of a prosperous and great city, and would have both these goods from their masters.

23.4. He ended by introducing the argument from advantage, reminding those who knew and teaching those who were ignorant, that for a city aiming at dominion and deeming itself worthy of great affairs there is no need of anything so much as of abundance of men, that it may suffice for all its wars, using its own arms and not, by hiring foreign armies, be exhausted along with its money; and for this reason, he said, the former kings had given a share of the citizenship to all strangers.

23.5. And if they should establish this law also, he said much youth would be reared for them from the freedmen, and the city would never lack its own arms, but would always have forces sufficient, even if it should be compelled to make war on all mankind.

23.6. And apart from the common advantage, the wealthiest of the Romans would be greatly benefited privately as well, if they should permit the freedmen to share in the citizenship — receiving their gratitude in assemblies and votings and the other political occasions, in the matters where they most have need, and leaving to their own descendants the clients sprung from the freedmen.

23.7. While he was saying such things, the patricians consented that the custom should come into the city; and to our times it continues to be guarded in the city as one of the sacred and immovable usages.

24.1. Since I have come to this part of the narrative, it seems necessary to me to set forth how the customs of the Romans concerning their slaves stood at that time, that neither the king who first attempted to make citizens of those who had been slaves, nor those who accepted the law, may be held in blame by anyone as men throwing away the noble things at random.

24.2. The acquisitions of servants by the Romans came about in the most just ways. For either, having bought from the public treasury those sold under the spear out of the spoils; or, with the general's consent, having along with the other profits the captives also for those who took them; or having bought from others who had become owners in the same ways — thus they had acquired their slaves.

24.3. Neither Tullius, then, who established the custom, nor those who accepted and preserved it, thought they were doing anything that was a cause of shame or of common harm, if to those deprived in war of country and freedom — who had become good toward those who enslaved them, or toward those who bought them from these — both these things should be supplied by their masters.

24.4. Most of them obtained their freedom freely on account of their merit; and this was the best manner of release from masters; but a few paid ransom gathered from holy and just earnings. But it is not so in our times; rather affairs have come to such confusion, and the noble things of the city of the Romans have become so dishonoured and foul, that some, having made money from brigandage and burglary and prostitution and every other base resource, buy their freedom with this money and are forthwith Romans;

24.5. others, having become accomplices and helpers of their masters in poisonings and murders and crimes against the gods or the commonwealth, receive these favours from them; others, that, receiving the corn distributed publicly each month, or whatever other bounty is given by the rulers to the needy citizens, they may bring it to those who gave them their freedom; and others through the

24.6. frivolity of their masters and empty love of glory. I myself, at any rate, know of some who have granted all their slaves to be free after their own deaths, that they may be called good men when dead, and that many may follow their biers as they are carried out, wearing the caps of freedom on their heads; among whom, as one might hear from those who knew, some marched in procession who had but lately come out of the prisons, malefactors who had committed deeds deserving ten thousand deaths. At these stains, so hard to wash out, the multitude, looking upon the city, are displeased and abhor the custom, as not befitting a sovereign city which deems itself worthy to rule

24.7. every region, to make such men citizens. One might find fault with many other customs also, well devised by the ancients but badly corrupted by men of the present day. For my part, I do not think this law ought to be abolished, lest some greater evil break out for the commonwealth through it; but I say that what can be corrected ought to be corrected, and that we ought not to overlook great reproaches and stains hard to wash out being introduced into the body politic.

24.8. And I would ask that the censors above all take forethought for this matter; or, failing that, the consuls; for there is need of some great magistrate; men who shall examine those who are freed each year — who they are, and why, and how they were freed — just as they examine the lives of the knights and of the senators; then those whom they find worthy of the city they shall enrol in tribes and permit to remain in the city; but the polluted and unclean tribe they shall cast out of the city, giving the act a seemly name, calling it a colony. These things, then, since the subject demands it, seemed to me necessary and just to say in answer to those who censure the customs of the Romans.

25.1. Tullius showed himself democratic not only in those measures of statecraft in which he was thought to lessen the authority of the senate and the power of the patricians, but also in those in which he diminished the royal power itself, taking away from himself the half of his authority.

25.2. For whereas the kings before him had claimed to bring all suits before themselves and decided all charges, both private and public, according to their own pleasure, he, separating public matters from private, himself made the decisions in wrongs that bore upon the commonwealth, but appointed private persons to be judges in private suits, fixing for them limits and

25.3. rules — the laws which he himself wrote. When his affairs in the city had received the best order, he came into a desire, by performing some illustrious deed, to leave an eternal memory of himself to posterity. And turning his thought to the monuments of the ancient kings and statesmen by which they advanced to renown and glory, he did not count that Assyrian woman blessed for the wall of Babylon, nor the kings of Egypt for the pyramids at Memphis, nor any other display of wealth and abundant labour of a ruler; but deeming all these to be small and short-lived and not worthy of zeal — deceptions of the eye, not true benefits to life and affairs, from which only the praise of being blessed followed for those who built them — and considering worthy of praise and emulation the works of judgment, of which very many enjoy the use and reap the benefits for the longest time, he admired above all such works the device of Amphictyon the Hellene, who, seeing the Greek race weak and easily destroyed by the surrounding barbarians, brought it together into the Amphictyonic council and festival named after him, establishing, besides the private laws which each city had, laws common to all, which they call Amphictyonic; by these they continued to be friends to one another, preserving their kinship more by deeds than by words, but grievous and fearful to the barbarians.

25.4. Taking the example from him, the Ionians who removed their dwelling from Europe to the coasts of Caria, and the Dorians who founded their cities about the same regions, built temples from common expenses — the Ionians at Ephesus the temple of Artemis, the Dorians at Triopium that of Apollo — where, coming together with their wives and children at the appointed times, they sacrificed in common and held festival together and celebrated games, equestrian and gymnastic and of the musical kind, and honoured the gods with common offerings.

25.5. And when they had viewed the spectacles and held festival and renewed their other friendly relations with one another, if any quarrel had arisen of city against city, sitting as judges they decided it; and concerning the war against the barbarians and concerning their harmony with one another they took common counsel.

25.6. Taking these and similar examples, he too became eager to unite and bring together all the cities sharing in the Latin race, that they might not, quarrelling and warring with one another, be robbed of their freedom by the neighbouring barbarians.

26.1. Having resolved on this, he summoned the most powerful men from each city, saying that he was calling them to be his counsellors about great and common affairs. And when they had come together, gathering the Roman senate and those who had come from the cities, he delivered a speech exhorting to concord, teaching that a fine thing it is for many cities to use one mind, but a shameful sight for kindred to quarrel with one another; and he declared concord the cause of strength to the weak, but mutual destruction the cause of lowliness and weakness even to the very strong.

26.2. Having set forth these things, he taught them that the Latins ought to rule the neighbouring peoples and to ordain justice for them, being Greeks set over barbarians; and that the Romans ought to hold the leadership of all the Latins, excelling them in the size of their city and the weight of their affairs, and having enjoyed a better providence of the divine power than they, through which they had advanced to so great a distinction.

26.3. Having set forth such things, he counselled them to build a temple of asylum from common expenses at Rome, in which the cities, coming together each year, should perform both private and common sacrifices and hold festivals at whatever times they should appoint; and, if any quarrel should arise among them with one another, they should settle it from the sacred rites, entrusting to the other cities the decision of the charges.

26.4. Setting forth these things and how many other goods they would have if they established a council-chamber, he persuaded all those present in the assembly; and after this he built, from the moneys which all the cities contributed, the temple of Artemis, the one situated on the largest of the hills in Rome, the Aventine; and he drew up the laws for the cities with one another and ordered the other matters concerning the festival and assembly, in what manner it should be celebrated.

26.5. And that no length of time might efface them, having made a bronze pillar, he wrote upon it both the resolutions of the councillors and the cities sharing in the council. This pillar remained down to my own time, lying in the temple of Artemis, with letters of the Greek characters which Greece anciently used. And this too one might make no small proof that those who founded Rome were not barbarians. For they would not have used Greek letters if they had been barbarians.

26.6. Of this king's measures of statecraft, then, these are the greatest and most brilliant that are recorded, along with many others lesser and more obscure; but his warlike deeds were those against the one nation of the Tyrrhenians, concerning which I am now about to relate.

27.1. After the death of Tarquinius the cities which had handed over the leadership to him no longer wished to keep their agreements, not thinking it right to obey Tullius, who was of humble birth, and believing that the dissension of the patricians with their leader would afford them great advantage.

27.2. Those called the Veientes began the revolt and answered the ambassadors who came from Tullius that they had no agreement with him, either concerning the cession of the leadership or concerning friendship and alliance. These having begun, the Caeretani followed and the Tarquinienses, and at last all Tyrrhenia was in arms.

27.3. This war continued to be waged for twenty years without interruption, both sides making many invasions of one another's territory with great armies and forming battle-lines one after another. But Tullius, succeeding in all the battles, as many as were fought with him both against the cities and against the whole nation, and being honoured with three most illustrious triumphs, at last compelled those who would not be ruled to take the bridle willingly.

27.4. In the twentieth year, then, the twelve cities, exhausted in the war both in men and in money, came together again and resolved to hand over the leadership to the Romans on the same terms they had voted before. And there came from every city the men chosen, with suppliant boughs, entrusting their cities to Tullius and asking that no irremediable measures be resolved upon concerning them.

27.5. Tullius said that for their folly and their impiety toward the gods — whom they had made guarantors of their agreements and then transgressed what had been covenanted — they deserved many great punishments; but that, by reason of the Romans' equity and moderation, since, acknowledging their wrong, they were deprecating his

27.6. anger with garlands and supplications, they should fare ill in nothing for the present. Saying this, he brought the war against them to an end, granting to the other cities, simply and without vindictive anger, to govern themselves as before and to enjoy their own possessions, remaining in the treaties written for them by King Tarquinius; but three of the cities — those which had revolted first and had drawn the others into making war on the Romans, the Caeretani and Tarquinienses and Veientes — he punished by taking away a portion of their land, which he allotted to those Romans who had but lately come over to the citizenship.

27.7. Having accomplished these things in peace and in wars, and having built two temples to Fortune, of whom throughout all his life he was thought to have enjoyed the good — the one in the so-called Forum Boarium, the other on the banks of the Tiber, which he surnamed Manly (as even now it is called by the Romans) — being far advanced in age and not far from his natural end, he was killed, the victim of a plot by Tarquinius his son-in-law and by his own daughter. I will relate also the manner of the plot, taking up briefly some of the things that happened before.

28.1. Tullius had two daughters born of his wife Tarquinia, whom King Tarquinius had betrothed to him. These maidens, when they came of marriageable age, he gave to the nephews of their mother, the grandsons of Tarquinius, matching the elder to the elder and the younger to the younger, thinking that thus they would best agree with those who received them.

28.2. But it happened that each of the sons-in-law was joined to a fortune contrary to himself, through unlikeness of character. For to Lucius, the elder, who was bold and self-willed and tyrannical in nature, came a good and modest and father-loving wife; while to Arruns, the younger, who had much of gentleness and good sense, the wedded woman was impious and father-hating and capable of any deed.

28.3. Thus it came about that each of the men was borne toward his own nature but drawn by his wife toward the contrary; for the wicked one, eager to expel his father-in-law from the kingship and contriving everything to this end, was turned aside by his wife, who entreated and lamented; while the equitable one, thinking he ought to do no wrong toward his father-in-law, but to wait until nature should lead him out of life, and not allowing his brother to do what was unjust, was drawn toward the contrary by his impious wife, who admonished and reviled him and reproached his unmanliness.

28.4. And when neither the supplications of the modest wife, persuading the unjust man to the best course, nor the exhortations of the wicked one, summoning him who was not by nature wicked to impious deeds, availed anything, but each was borne toward his own nature and deemed grievous the wife who did not wish the same things — to the one it remained to lament and bear her own fate, but to the all-daring woman to be angry and to seek release from him with whom she lived.
28.5. Then the woman, evil in nature, growing desperate and thinking that her sister's husband best suited her own ways, sent for him as though to converse about a necessary matter,

29.1. and when he had come, ordering those within to withdraw, that she might speak with him alone, she said: "May I, Tarquinius, with frankness and without danger speak all that I think concerning our common advantage, and will you keep to yourself whatever words you hear? Or is it better for me to be silent and not bring into the open secret counsels?"

29.2. When Tarquinius bade her say what she wished and gave her pledges by oaths, such as she chose, that he would keep the words within himself, no longer ashamed she said to him: "How long, Tarquinius, do you intend to endure being deprived of the kingship? Were you sprung from humble and obscure ancestors, and is it for this reason that you do not deem yourself worthy to think highly of yourself? But all know that to your ancient ancestors, who were Greeks and descended from Heracles, belonged the sovereign rule of prosperous Corinth for many generations, as I hear; and to your grandfather Tarquinius, who removed his dwelling from the Tyrrhenians, it fell to reign over this city through his virtue; of whom you, being the elder grandson, ought to inherit not only the wealth but also the kingship.

29.3. Or did you not get a body sufficient to do all that befits a king, through weakness and ugliness? But strength is yours, such as belongs to the best endowed, and a form worthy of the royal line. Or is it neither of these, but does youth, still weak and far from prudent judgment, draw you back, for which reason you do not deem yourself fit to manage public affairs — you who are not many years short of being fifty? Men are by nature best able to judge who are about this very age.

29.4. Come then — but does the nobility of him who holds affairs, and his good relations with the most powerful of the citizens, on account of which he is not easily attacked, compel you to endure? But both of these too chance to be in a bad state for him, and you yourself are not ignorant of it. And surely the boldness and love of danger are in your character, which most of all he who is to be king needs. There belong to you also sufficient wealth and many friends and many other great resources for affairs.

29.5. Why, then, do you still delay and await the moment that comes of itself, which will come to you bringing the kingship though you have done nothing to that end — after the death of Tullius, I suppose? As though Fortune awaited the delays of men, or our nature brought to each his end according to his age, and the end of all human affairs did not lie in an obscure and hard-to-conjecture conclusion!

29.6. I will say it then with frankness, even if you will call me bold — what seems to me the cause of your reaching after no ambition nor glory. A wife is with you in no way like your own ways, who, charming and bewitching you, has rendered you soft, and you will become, without knowing it, from a man into a nothing; just as for me there is a timorous husband with nothing of a man, who makes me lowly though I am worthy of great things and fair in body, but withered by him.

29.7. But if it had fallen to you to take me as wife and to me to obtain you as husband, we should not have lived out so long a time in private life. Why, then, do we not correct the defect of fortune by changing our marriages — you removing your own wife from life, and I doing the same to my husband? And when, these having been dispatched, we come together into one, then in security we will plan the rest, having removed out of the way the things that grieve us. For even if one shrinks from other wrongs, for the sake of a kingship there is no offence in daring all things."

30.1. While Tullia was saying such things, Tarquinius gladly accepted her proposals, and at once, having given her pledges and received them, and having performed the preliminary rites of these impious nuptials, he departed. No long time after this, the elder of the daughters of Tullius and the younger of the Tarquinii died by the same calamities.

30.2. Here again I am compelled to make mention of Fabius and to convict his carelessness about the examination of the times. For in dealing with the death of Arruns he errs not in one respect only — which I also said before, that he has written that Arruns was the son of Tarquinius — but also in another, that he says he was buried, after death, by his mother Tanaquil, who could not possibly have been still living in those times.

30.3. For it was shown at the outset that Tanaquil was in her seventy-fifth year when King Tarquinius died; if, then, to the seventy-five years another forty be added — for in the Annals we have received that Arruns died in the fortieth year of the rule of Tullius — Tanaquil will be a hundred and fifteen years old. So small is the diligence about the examination of truth in his histories.
30.4. After this deed Tarquinius, delaying no longer, took Tullia to wife, neither her father confirming the marriage nor her mother consenting, but having received her from herself.

30.5. And when the impious and murderous natures had been blended together, they contrived to expel Tullius from the kingship, if he should not be willing to surrender the rule voluntarily, gathering associations and inviting those of the patricians who were estranged from the king and from the democratic measures, and buying with money the poorest of the common multitude, who had no care for justice; and they did not even do each of these things in secret.

30.6. Tullius, seeing this, was vexed, fearing for himself lest he should suffer some harm by being forestalled; and he was indignant not least because he would be compelled to make war on his daughter and son-in-law and to take vengeance as from enemies. Often, with his friends, he summoned Tarquinius to conference, now reproaching, now admonishing, now persuading him to do no wrong against himself; and when Tarquinius did not give heed but said he would state his just claims against him before the senate, Tullius summoned the council and said:

30.7. "Senators, Tarquinius, gathering associations against me and eager to expel me from the rule, has become manifest to me. I wish, in the presence of you all, to learn from him what private harm he has suffered, or what wrong to the city he sees being done by me, that he contrives these things against me. Answer, then, Tarquinius, hiding nothing — what accusation you have to bring against me, since you saw fit that these men should hear."

31.1. Tarquinius says to him: "My speech is brief, Tullius, and just; and for this reason I chose to bring it before these men. Tarquinius, being my grandfather, acquired the rule of the Romans, taking upon himself many and great struggles on its behalf. He having died, I am his successor according to the common laws of all, both Greeks and barbarians; and it belongs to me, as to all others who succeed to their grandfathers' estates, to inherit not only the wealth, but also

31.2. his kingship. But the wealth left by him you have handed over to me, while of the kingship you rob me and have now held it so long a time, not having received it justly. For neither did interreges appoint you, nor did the senate cast a vote for you, nor did you obtain this authority by lawful elections, as did my grandfather and all the kings before him; but the homeless and needy rabble, and that which had lost its citizen rights through condemnations or debts, which cared for nothing public, you hired with pay and corrupted in every way; and not even then did you say you were procuring the rule for yourself, but pretended you would guard it for us, who were orphans and infants; and you came to power, and in the hearing of all you acknowledged that, when we should come to manhood, to me, as the

31.3. elder, you would hand over the rule. You ought, then, if you wished to do what is just, when you handed over to me the house of my grandfather, to have given back the kingship along with the wealth, using as examples the deeds of good and noble guardians, all those who, having received royal children orphaned of their fathers, when they came to manhood rightly and justly restored to them their fathers' and

31.4. ancestral rules. But if I did not yet seem to you to be of fit judgment, but still, by reason of the youth of my age, not capable of governing so great a city, when I came to the strongest prime of body and judgment, being thirty years old, you ought, together with the marriage of your daughter, to have committed to me also the affairs of the city. At that very age you yourself both began to be guardian of our house and to take charge of the kingship."

32.1. "For if you had done these things, it would have remained to you, first, to be called pious and just; then, to reign together with me and to share in every honour, and to be called benefactor and father and saviour and all those most honoured names which are bestowed by men upon noble deeds; and not now, for this the four-and-fortieth year, to rob me of what is mine, you who have got neither a maimed body nor a foolish mind.
