Then you dare to ask me what terrible thing I have suffered that I count you an enemy, and why

32.2. I accuse you? Answer me, then, Tullius, for what reason you do not think me worthy to inherit my grandfather's honours, and what specious pretext for the deprivation you allege. Is it because you do not think me a legitimate offspring of his line, but some supposititious and bastard child? Why, then, were you guardian of one alien to the family, and why did you give back the house to me when I came to manhood? Or because you still think me an orphan child and unable to manage public affairs — I who am not far from fifty? Lay aside, then, the irony of your shameless

32.3. questions, and cease at last from being wicked; but if you have anything just to say to this, I am ready to entrust the matter to these men as judges, than whom you could not name other better men in the city; but if, slipping away from here — which is ever your custom — you flee to the mob you have demagogued, I will not permit you. For I am prepared both to state what is just and, if you do not yield, to do what is forcible."

33.1. When he had ceased, Tullius, taking up the speech, spoke thus: "It seems, senators, that being a man one must expect all the unexpected things and deem nothing incredible, when even me this Tarquinius is eager to remove from the rule — whom I, taking up as an infant and plotted against by his enemies, saved and reared, and, when he came to manhood, thought fit to take as my kinsman, and, if I should suffer anything, was about to leave as successor of all my possessions. But since everything has fallen out for me against my expectation, and I am accused as though I myself were the wrongdoer, I will lament my fortune later,

33.2. but now I will state my just claims against him. I took the guardianship of you, Tarquinius, when you were left infants, not willingly, but compelled by the circumstances; since those who disputed the kingship had openly killed your grandfather, and were said to be secretly plotting against you and his other kinsmen; and all your relations agreed that, if those men got the rule, they would not leave even a seed of the line of Tarquinius. There was no other protector or guardian of you save a woman, your father's mother, and she through old age herself needing other guardians; but you were left to me alone as guardian of your desolation — me whom you now call alien and in no way related.

33.3. Yet, standing over such affairs, I both punished the murderers of your grandfather and brought you to manhood, and, there being no male offspring, I chose to make you masters of my own possessions. You have the account of the guardianship, Tarquinius, and you could not attempt to say that I lie in any of these things.

34.1. But concerning the kingship — since this is what you accuse me of — hear both how I obtained it and for what reasons I yield it neither to you nor to any other. When I took the charge of the city, perceiving that certain plots were being formed against me, I wished to hand over affairs to the people; and gathering all into an assembly, I gave them back the rule, exchanging for this envied leadership, which has more griefs than pleasures, a quiet free from danger.

34.2. The Romans did not endure my wishing to do this, nor did they think fit to appoint any other master of public affairs, but held me back and gave me the kingship by casting their vote — their own possession, Tarquinius, not yours;

34.3. just as they also brought your grandfather to power, though he was a stranger and in no way related to the former king; and yet King Ancus Marcius left sons in their prime, not grandsons and infants, as Tarquinius left you. But if it were a common law for all that those who succeed to the manifest property and wealth of departed kings should, along with these, receive also their kingships, your grandfather Tarquinius would not have received the leadership when Ancus died, but the elder of his sons.

34.4. But the people of the Romans called to power not the successor of the father, but the one worthy of the rule; for it held that wealth belongs to those who acquire it, but the kingship to those who give it; and that the former, when its owners suffer anything, it befits their successors by birth or by will to receive, but the latter, when those who have received it depart, those who gave it should hold — unless you have some such claim to bring, that your grandfather received the kingship on certain express terms, so as both to hold it himself inalienably and to leave it to you his descendants, and the people had no

34.5. authority to take it from you and give it to me. For if you have any such thing to say, why do you not bring the agreements into the open? But you could not. And if I obtained it not in the best manner, as you say, neither chosen by the interreges nor with the senate handing me affairs nor the other things being done according to law — these men, I suppose, I wrong, and not you, and by these men I deserve to be deprived of the rule, not by

34.6. you. But neither these men nor any other do I wrong. Witness of the authority justly given to me then and now possessed is the time, in which, having held it for forty years, no Roman ever thought me to do wrong, nor did anyone attempt to expel me from the rule, neither the people nor the senate.

35.1. But, that I may let all these things go and come to grips with your words — if I were robbing you of your grandfather's deposit and were holding your kingship against all justice among men, you ought, going to those who gave me the authority, to be indignant and to accuse both me, that I hold what does not belong to me, and those who gave it, that they bestowed on me what was another's; for you would easily have persuaded them, if you had anything just to say.

35.2. But if you did not trust this argument, and thought the city was unjustly ruled by me and that you yourself were better fitted to take the charge of public affairs, it befitted you to do those things: making an examination of my errors and reckoning up your own deeds, to call me to a trial; neither of which you did, but, so many years afterward, as though awakened from a long drunkenness, you now come accusing me — and not even now where you ought.

35.3. For it does not befit you to say these things here — and be not vexed at me for saying this, senators; for I do not say it taking the judgment from you, but wishing to display this man's calumny — but you ought, having first given me notice, to gather the people into an assembly and there to accuse me. But since you have shunned this, I will do it concerning you, and, summoning the people, I will furnish you a judge of whatever you accuse me, and will give it back again to them to decide which of us is the better fitted to hold the rule; and whatever all these men shall judge that I ought to do, I will do.

35.4. And against you this is enough; for it is the same thing to say many just things to senseless adversaries and to say few; for words are by nature unable to carry that which will make them good men.

36.1. But of you I have marvelled, senators, if there are any wishing to remove me from the rule and combined against me with this man. I would gladly learn from them for what wrong they make war on me and at which of my deeds they are vexed. Is it because they know that many men under my rule have perished untried, or been deprived of country, or lost their estates, or unjustly met with some other calamity? Or, while they can name none of these tyrannical wrongs done by me, are they aware of some outrages by me against wedded wives, or insults to maiden daughters, or some other licentiousness toward a free person? Justly indeed, if I have committed any such thing, should I be deprived at once both of the rule and of life.

36.2. Come then — but am I arrogant and, through harshness, oppressive, and can no one bear the self-will I have used in the rule? Yet which of the kings before me lived so moderately in authority and so humane toward all the citizens, as a gentle father using his own sons? — I who did not even wish to hold all the authority which you gave me, preserving the traditions of your fathers, but, having established laws concerning the most important matters, which you all ratified, gave back to you to give and receive justice according to these, and myself was examined first by the laws I fixed against others, obeying like a private man; and of wrongs I did not become the judge of all, but assigned to you to decide the private suits — which none of the former kings did.

36.3. But it seems there is no wrong on account of which any are displeased with me, but my benefactions to the common multitude seem to grieve you, concerning which I have often defended myself to you. But there is no need of these words now; if it seems that this Tarquinius will take better care of public affairs by receiving them, I do not begrudge the city a better ruler; and, giving back the rule to the people who gave it to me and becoming a private man, I will try to make plain to all that I both know how to rule well and am able to be ruled with moderation."

37.1. Having discoursed thus and brought into great shame those combined against him, he dissolved the meeting; and after this, calling the heralds, he ordered them, going through all the lanes, to summon the people into an assembly.

37.2. When the crowd of the city had run together into the Forum, coming forward upon the platform he delivered a long and moving harangue, recounting his warlike deeds, those he had performed while Tarquinius lived and those after his death, and going over his measures of statecraft one by one, from which the commonwealth was thought to have received many great benefits.

37.3. And when much praise met each of his statements, and all were eager to learn for what reasons he was saying these things, at the end he said that Tarquinius accused him of holding unjustly a kingship that belonged to himself; for his grandfather, dying, had left to him the rule along with the wealth, and the people had no authority to give what belonged to another to

37.4. another. When there arose from all an outcry and indignation at this, ordering them to be silent, he asked them not to be vexed nor indignant at the speech, but, if Tarquinius had anything just to say, to call him; and, being informed, if they should find him wronged or better fitted to rule, to hand over to him the protection of the city; for he himself, he said, withdrew from the rule and gave it back to its owners, from whom he had received it.

37.5. When he had said this and wished to come down from the platform, there arose from all an outcry and many entreaties with lamentations that he should yield the rule to no one; and some of them cried out to stone Tarquinius. He, then, fearing summary justice, since the crowds were already rushing upon him, went off in flight together with his companions; but the whole multitude, escorting Tullius with joy and applause and much auspicious acclamation, brought him to his house.

38.1. When Tarquinius had failed in this attempt also, distressed that no help had come to him from the senate, in which he had most trusted, for some time he kept to his house, conversing only with his companions. Then, his wife declaring her opinion that he should no longer be soft nor shrink back, but, casting words aside, should proceed to deeds — first having obtained a reconciliation through friends with Tullius, that, trusting him as one become a friend, Tullius might guard against him less — and thinking that she had suggested the best course, he pretended to repent of what had happened and, beseeching much through friends, asked Tullius to be forgiving.

38.2. And very easily persuading the man, who was by nature easily reconciled and did not think fit to wage implacable war against a daughter and son-in-law, when he had got the suitable occasion, the people being dispersed about the fields for the harvesting of the crops, he went out with his companions, who had swords beneath their cloaks, and, giving the axes to certain attendants and himself taking the royal robe and bringing with him the other insignia of the rule, he came into the Forum and, standing before the senate-house, ordered the herald to summon the senators to the council. There were ready, by arrangement, about the Forum many of the patricians privy to him in the deed

38.3. and urging him on. They, then, were assembling; and to Tullius, who was at his house, someone came and said that Tarquinius had come forth in royal robe and was summoning the senators to the council. And he, marvelling at his boldness, came forth from his house more quickly than wisely, with not many about him. Coming into the council-chamber and seeing Tarquinius seated on the royal chair and having the rest of the royal adornment,

38.4. he said: "Who, most polluted of men, permitted you to take this guise?" And Tarquinius, taking him up, said: "Your own boldness and shamelessness, Tullius — you who, not being even free, but a slave born of a slave-woman whom my grandfather acquired from among the captives, dared to declare yourself king of the Romans." When Tullius heard this, embittered at the speech beyond what was expedient, he rushed at him as if to raise him from the seat.

38.5. And Tarquinius, glad to see this, sprang up from the chair, and seizing the old man, who cried out and called upon his attendants, carried him off. Having got outside the senate-house, lifting him up aloft — being a man in the prime of body and strong — he hurled him down the steps of the senate-house, those that lead to the assembly-place.

38.6. The old man, with difficulty rising from his fall, when he saw all the surroundings full of the company of Tarquinius and a great desertion of his own friends, departed groaning, with a few holding him up and escorting him, streaming with much blood and in evil case throughout his whole body from the fall.

39.1. What followed — terrible to hear, but marvellous and incredible to have been done — is recorded as the deed of his impious daughter. For having learned of her father's entrance into the senate-house and being eager to know what end affairs would take, sitting in her carriage she came to the Forum. Learning what had happened, and beholding Tarquinius standing on the step before the senate-house, she was the first to salute him as king with a loud voice and prayed to the gods that for the advantage of the city of the Romans he might hold the rule.

39.2. And when the others also who had helped to establish the rule had saluted him as king, taking him aside alone she said: "The first things, Tarquinius, have been done by you as was needful; but to hold the kingship securely while Tullius lives is not possible for you. For he will again demagogue the mob against you, if he survive any portion at all of this day; and you know how well-disposed all the common people are to him. But, before he enters his house, send those who shall dispatch him and put him out of the way."

39.3. Having said this and sitting again in her carriage, she went off. Tarquinius, thinking that in this too the most impious of women advised rightly, sends certain of his servants against him with swords; who, with great speed accomplishing the intervening road, overtook Tullius, who was already near his house, and slaughtered him. While the body was still lying freshly slain and twitching,

39.4. his daughter arrived. The lane through which the carriage had to pass being very narrow, the mules, seeing the corpse, were thrown into confusion, and the muleteer who led them, suffering something at the piteous sight, stopped and looked toward his mistress. When she asked what he meant by not driving the team on, he said: "Do you not see, Tullia, your father lying dead, and that there is no other passage save through the corpse?"

39.5. But she, embittered, snatching up the footstool from beneath her feet, hurled it at the muleteer and said: "Will you not drive on, accursed wretch, even through the dead?" And he, groaning more at the calamity than at the blow, drove the mules by force over the corpse. This lane, formerly called Orbius, from that terrible and abominable event is called Wicked by the Romans in their native tongue.

40.1. Such was the end that befell Tullius, after holding the kingship forty-four years. The Romans say that this man was the first to disturb the ancestral customs and usages, having received the rule not from the senate and the people, as all before him, but from the people alone, courting the poor with bribes and corruptions and many other flatteries; and this is the truth.

40.2. For in former times, whenever a king died, the people gave the authority to the council of the senate to establish whatever constitution it preferred; and the senate appointed interreges, and they set up as king the best man, whether from the natives, or from the citizens, or from strangers. If, then, the senate approved the one chosen by them, and the people ratified him by vote, and the auspices confirmed it, this man received the rule; but if any of these was lacking, they named another, and a third, if it should not befall the second also that the things from men and

40.3. the things from the gods were beyond reproach. But Tullius, having at the outset taken the guise of a royal guardian, as I said before, then having won the people over by certain acts of humanity, was declared king by them alone. Being an equitable and moderate man, he dissolved by his later deeds the calumnies arising from his not having done everything according to the laws, and gave many the supposition that, had he not been killed sooner, he would have changed the form of the constitution into a democracy.

40.4. And for this reason chiefly some of the patricians are said to have joined in plotting against him; and being unable by any other means to overthrow his authority, to have brought Tarquinius to power and helped to establish the rule for him, wishing to weaken the common people, who had got no small strength from the constitution of Tullius, and to recover their own dignity, which they formerly had.

40.5. When there arose much tumult throughout the whole city and lamentation at the death of Tullius, Tarquinius, fearing lest, if the corpse were carried through the Forum, as is the custom of the Romans, with the royal adornment and the other things which law prescribes for royal burials, some movement against himself should arise from the common people before he had securely strengthened the rule, did not permit any of the customary rites to be performed for him; but the wife of Tullius, with a few of her friends — she being the daughter of Tarquinius the former king — by night carried the body out of the city, as that of some chance person; and, lamenting much her own and his fortune and uttering ten thousand curses against the son-in-law and the daughter, hid the body in the earth.

40.6. Returning home from the tomb and surviving one day after the burial, on the following night she died. The manner of her death, whatever it was, was unknown to most; some said that, through grief, she gave up life by her own hand and so died; others, that she was made away with by the son-in-law and the daughter, on account of her sympathy and goodwill toward her husband. For these reasons, then, the body of Tullius did not chance upon a royal burial and a conspicuous monument; but his deeds enjoy eternal memory for all time.

40.7. Another divine work also made plain that the man was beloved of the gods, by reason of which even the mythical and incredible supposition about his birth was believed by many to be true, as I said before. For in the temple of Fortune which he himself built, an image of him, of wood overlaid with gold, when a conflagration occurred and all the rest was destroyed, alone remained unharmed by the fire. And even now the temple and all that is in it — all that was done after the conflagration to restore the ancient adornment — are plainly of the new craft; but the image is of ancient workmanship, such as it was before; for it still continues to receive veneration from the Romans. So much concerning Tullius we have received.

41.1. After him Lucius Tarquinius takes over the rule of the Romans, holding it not according to the laws but having seized it by arms, in the fourth year of the sixty-first Olympiad, the one in which Agatharchus the Corcyrean won the foot-race, Thericles being archon at Athens.

41.2. This man, despising the common multitude, and despising also the patricians by whom he had been brought to power, and confounding and corrupting the customs and laws and all the native order with which the former kings had adorned the city, transformed the rule into an avowed tyranny.

41.3. And first he established about himself a guard of the boldest men bearing swords and spears, both natives and foreigners, who, lodging by night about the royal court and following him by day, wherever he went, afforded him much security against those who would plot against him. Then he made his goings-forth neither continuous nor regular, but rare and unexpected; and he transacted public business for the most part at home, and in the presence of his most intimate associates, but few things in the Forum.

41.4. He permitted none who wished to approach, unless he himself should summon someone; nor was he gracious or gentle to those who approached, but, as a tyrant indeed, heavy and harsh in anger and more fearful than cheerful to behold; and the judgments concerning disputed contracts he made not according to justice and the laws, but according to his own dispositions. For these reasons the Romans give him the surname Superbus, which in our tongue means "the arrogant"; and his grandfather they called Priscus, that is, as we should say, "the elder"; for he was of the same name in both names as the younger.

42.1. When he supposed that he now held the rule firmly, having prepared from his associates the most wicked, through them he brought into accusations and capital trials many of the distinguished men — first those disposed hostilely toward him, who were unwilling that Tullius should fall from the rule; then also of the others, those whom he supposed deemed the change grievous and those who had much wealth.

42.2. And those who brought them under the trials, charging some on one false accusation and some on another, but most of all charging them with plotting against the king, accused them before him as judge. He condemned some to death, others to exile, and, taking away the wealth of those slain and those expelled, paid out some small portion to the accusers,

42.3. but himself kept the greater part. Many, then, of the powerful, before being convicted of the trials brought against them, knowing for what reasons they were plotted against, willingly left the city to the tyrant; and they became far more numerous than the others. There were some too who were secretly destroyed by him, seized from their houses and from the fields, men worthy of record, of whom not even the bodies appeared.

42.4. When he had destroyed the best part of the senate by deaths and perpetual exiles, he himself established another senate, bringing forward his own associates to the honours of those who had departed. And not even to these men did he permit to do or to say anything that he himself had not commanded.

42.5. So that all the senators who were left in the council, of those enrolled under Tullius — who till then had been at variance with the commons and had thought the change of constitution would be for their own good (for such promises Tarquinius held out to them, deceiving and cheating them) — then learning that they no longer had a share in any public matter, but that they too, along with the commons, had been deprived of free speech, lamented and suspected the future to be more terrible than the present, but were compelled to be content with the present, having no power to prevent what was being done.

43.1. Seeing this, the commons supposed that they were suffering justly and rejoiced through simplicity, as though the tyranny would be grievous to those men alone, but free of danger to themselves. But to them too, not long after, came still more grievous things. For the laws written by Tullius, by which they received justice from one another on equal terms and were in no way harmed by the patricians, as before, in matters of contracts, he abolished all; and he did not even leave the tablets on which they were written, but, ordering these too to be taken down from the Forum, he destroyed them.

43.2. Then he abolished the contributions from the assessments and restored the original method; and whenever he had need of money, the poorest man paid the same sum as the richest. This measure consumed much of the common multitude, who were compelled, at the very first contribution, to pay ten drachmae per head. And all the gatherings which formerly took place — of villagers or members of curiae or neighbours, both in the city and in the fields, for sacred rites and sacrifices common to all — he proclaimed should no longer be held, lest many coming together to the same place should make secret counsels with one another about the overthrow of the rule.

43.3. And he had spies scattered in many places and searchers-out of what was said and done, who escaped the notice of the many, who, descending into conversation with those near them and sometimes themselves speaking against the tyrant, made trial of each one's mind; and then those whom they perceived to be vexed at the established state of things they denounced to the tyrant; and the punishments against those convicted were bitter and inexorable.

44.1. And it did not suffice him to transgress the law against the commons in these ways only; but, choosing out from the multitude as much as was faithful to himself and serviceable for warlike needs, he compelled the rest to labour at the works in the city, thinking it the greatest danger for monarchs when the most wicked and poorest of the citizens are at leisure, and at the same time having the desire, during his own rule, to complete the works left half-finished by his grandfather: to carry the drainage-channels for the waters, which the elder Tarquinius had begun to dig, down to the river, and to enclose with roofed colonnades the amphitheatrical hippodrome, which had nothing outside its foundations.

44.2. At these works, then, all the poor laboured, receiving from him a moderate ration of corn: some quarrying stone, some cutting timber, some driving the wagons that carried these, some themselves bearing the loads on their shoulders; others mining the underground tunnels and forming the vaults within them and raising the colonnades; and serving these artisans who did this work were smiths and carpenters and stonemasons, withdrawn from their private occupations and held to the public needs.

44.3. The people, worn down at these works, took no respite; so that the patricians, seeing their hardships and servitudes, rejoiced in their turn and forgot their own griefs; for neither side attempted to prevent what was being done.

45.1. Reckoning that for those who have got their rule not according to the laws but acquired it by arms there is need not only of a native guard but also of a foreign one, Tarquinius was eager to make the most distinguished man of the Latin nation, and the most powerful of all, his friend by joining him to himself through the marriage of his daughter. This man was called Octavius Mamilius and traced his descent to Telegonus, the son of Odysseus and Circe, and dwelt in the city of Tusculum, and was thought to be sagacious in political matters as few are and capable of commanding in wars.

45.2. Having this man as friend, and through him gaining over the best of those managing public affairs in each city, he then attempted to make trial of wars in the open field also and to lead out an army against the Sabines, who were unwilling to be subject to his commands but thought they had been released from their agreements ever since Tullius died, with whom they had made the agreements.

45.3. Knowing this, he gave notice through messengers that those accustomed to deliberate on behalf of the Latin commonwealth should come to the assembly held at Ferentinum, fixing a certain day, as one about to take counsel with them concerning common and great affairs.

45.4. They, then, were present, but Tarquinius himself, who had summoned them, was late. And when much time had passed as they sat, and the matter seemed to most an insult, a certain man dwelling in the city of Corilla, powerful in wealth and friends and valiant in war and not unable to deliver a political speech, Turnus Herdonius by name — at variance with Mamilius through rivalry over public affairs and hating Tarquinius on account of Mamilius, because he had thought fit to take that man as kinsman instead of himself — made a great accusation of Tarquinius, recounting both the other deeds of the man, in which a certain self-will and harshness seemed to be present, and his not being present at the meeting himself, the very one who had summoned it, when all the others were present.

45.5. When Mamilius defended him and ascribed Tarquinius's delay to certain necessary causes and asked that the meeting be put off to the following day, the presidents of the Latins, persuaded, adjourned the council.

46.1. On the next day Tarquinius was present, and when the council had assembled, after a few words concerning the delay, he immediately made speeches about the leadership, as belonging to him by right, since his grandfather Tarquinius had held it, having acquired it by war, and he produced the agreements made by the cities with that man.

46.2. Having delivered a long discourse concerning his right and the agreements, and having promised that he would greatly benefit the cities if they remained in the friendship, he at length tried to persuade them to join in a campaign against the Sabine nation.

46.3. When he had ceased speaking, Turnus, the one who had reproached him for his lateness, came forward and would not allow the councillors to yield the leadership to the man, as belonging to him neither by right nor to be given for the advantage of the Latins; and he delivered many words on both points, saying that the agreements which they had made with his grandfather, handing over the leadership, had been dissolved after that man's death, because it had not been added in writing to the agreements that the same gift should belong also to the descendants of Tarquinius; and declaring the man who claimed to inherit his grandfather's gifts the most lawless and wicked of all men, and recounting his deeds which he had performed in order to

46.4. seize the rule of the Romans. Having delivered many terrible accusations of him, at the end he taught that he did not even hold the kingship of the Romans according to the laws, having received it from willing subjects like the kings before him, but having prevailed by arms and force and established a tyrannical monarchy; that he killed some of the citizens, drove others from their country, cut off the property of others, and took away the free speech and freedom of all at once. He said it was great folly and god-stricken madness to expect and believe any good and humane thing from a wicked and impious character — as though one who had not spared his nearest and dearest kin would spare strangers; and he urged that, while they had not yet taken the bridle of slavery, they should fight that he might not put it on, conjecturing from the terrible things which others had suffered what would befall themselves.

47.1. When Turnus had made such an attack and the multitude had been greatly moved by the words, Tarquinius asked for the following day for his defence and, having got it, when the council had been dissolved, calling together his most intimate associates, he considered with them in what manner he should deal with the matter. The rest, then, suggested the words he should say in his defence and reckoned up the ways in which he should win over the multitude. But Tarquinius himself said there was no need of any of these things for the affair, and declared his own opinion: not to refute the charges, but

47.2. to make away with the accuser himself. When all praised the opinion, having arranged with them the matters concerning the attack, he undertook a thing least able to fall within human foresight and guard. For, finding out the most wicked of the servants who conveyed the baggage-animals and the gear of Turnus, and corrupting them with money, he persuaded them to take from him by night many swords and bring them into the lodging of their master and to lay them away, hidden among the baggage.

47.3. On the next day, when the assembly had gathered, coming forward, he said that the defence concerning the charges was brief, and made the accuser himself judge of all the charges. "For this Turnus, councillors," he said, "having become judge of all those things of which he now accuses me, himself acquitted me, when he wished to take my daughter to wife.

47.4. But when he was rejected from the marriage, as was natural — for who of those having sense would have spurned Mamilius, the noblest and most powerful of the Latins, and thought fit to take as kinsman this man, who cannot trace his line even to a third grandfather? — vexed at this, he now comes accusing me. But he ought, if he knew me to be such as he now charges, not to have been eager then to take me as father-in-law; and if he thought me good, when he asked for my daughter, not now to accuse me as wicked.

47.5. And concerning myself I say so much; but for you, councillors, who run the greatest of dangers, it is not now to be considered whether I am good or wicked — for this it will be possible for you to consider even afterward — but concerning your own safety and the freedom of your countries. For you, the foremost in the cities and those who manage public affairs, are being plotted against by this fine demagogue, who has prepared, having killed the most distinguished of you, to attack the rule of the Latins, and has come for this very

47.6. purpose. And these things I say not conjecturing, but knowing exactly, an information having come to me in the past night by one of those who shared in the conspiracy. And I will furnish you an indisputable proof of my words in deed, if you are willing to go to his lodging, by showing the weapons hidden in it."

48.1. When he said this, all cried out and, fearing for the men, asked that the matter be proved and that he not deceive them. And Turnus, as one who had not foreknown the plot, gladly said he accepted the examination and called upon the presidents to the search of the lodging, and said that one of two things ought to happen: either that he himself should die, if he were found to have prepared weapons beyond those for the road, or that the man who had lied against him should

48.2. undergo punishment. This seemed good; and those who went to his lodging found among the baggage the swords hidden by the servants. After this, no longer permitting Turnus to obtain a hearing, they cast him into a certain pit and, heaping the earth upon him while he yet lived, destroyed him forthwith.

48.3. And Tarquinius, having praised before the assembly as a common benefactor of the cities, for having saved the best men, they make him leader of the nation on the same terms on which they had earlier made Tarquinius his grandfather and afterward Tullius; and writing the agreements on pillars and cutting victims over the keeping of the covenants, they dissolved the council.

49.1. Having obtained the leadership of the Latins, Tarquinius sent embassies also to the cities of the Hernicans and to those of the Volscians, inviting these too to friendship and alliance. The Hernicans, then, all voted to make the alliance; but of the Volscian nation only two cities accepted the invitations, the Ecetrani and the Antiates. And taking forethought that the agreements should remain for all time for the cities, Tarquinius resolved to designate a common temple of the Romans and Latins and Hernicans and those of the Volscians enrolled in the alliance, that, coming together each year to the appointed place, they might hold festival and feast together and share in common sacred rites.

49.2. When all had gladly accepted the matter, he designated a place where they should hold the assembly, a high mountain situated almost in the middle of the nations, which overlooks the city of the Albans, on which he enacted that festivals should be held every year and that there should be a truce for all toward all, and that common sacrifices should be performed to the so-called Latiarian Jupiter and common feasts held, ordering what each city should furnish for the rites and what portion each should receive. The cities that shared in the festival and the sacrifice were forty-seven.

49.3. These festivals and sacrifices the Romans perform down to our times, calling them the Latin Festival; and the cities that share in the rites bring to them, some lambs, some cheeses, some a measure of milk, and some some similar kind of cake; and one bull being sacrificed in common by all, each receives its appointed portion. They sacrifice on behalf of all, and the Romans hold the leadership of the rites.

50.1. When he had strengthened his rule by these alliances too, he resolved to lead out an army against the Sabines, having chosen of the Romans themselves those whom he least suspected, if they should become masters of arms, of aiming at freedom, and adding the force that had come from the allies, which was much greater than the citizen force.

50.2. Having ravaged their fields and defeated in battle those who came to meet him, he led the force against the so-called Pometini, who inhabited the city of Suessa and were thought to be the most prosperous of all their neighbours, and through their great prosperity grievous and burdensome to all, charging them with certain plunderings and brigandages, for which, when asked for satisfaction, they gave arrogant answers. They were ready, awaiting the war and in arms.

50.3. Joining battle with them about the borders and killing many, and routing the rest and shutting them up within their wall, when they no longer came forth from the city, he encamped beside them and surrounded them with a ditch and palisade and made continuous assaults upon the walls. Those within for a time fought back and held out long against the hardship; but when supplies failed them, weakening in body and getting no reinforcement nor rest, but toiling themselves both day and night, they are taken by storm.

50.4. Having become master of the city, he destroyed those in arms, but permitted the soldiers to carry off as captives their wives and children and those who survived to become prisoners and the multitude of servants, not even easy to count, and to drive and carry off the other property of the city, whatever each might happen upon, both within the wall and in the fields; but the silver and gold, as much as was found, he gathered into one place and, taking out the tenth for the building of a temple, divided the remaining moneys among the soldiers.
50.5. So great, then, was the silver and gold that was taken, that each of the soldiers received five minae of silver, and the silver tithed for the gods came to not less than four hundred talents.

51.1. While he was still tarrying at Suessa, someone came announcing that the best youth of the Sabines had gone forth and, having invaded the Roman territory with two great armies, were plundering the fields — one having pitched its camp near Eretum, the other about Fidenae; and that, unless some force should oppose them, all there would be lost.

51.2. When he heard this, leaving at Suessa a small part of the army with orders to guard the spoils and the baggage, taking up the rest of the force light-equipped, he led it against those encamped near Eretum and pitched his camp on high ground, leaving a small space between. When it seemed good to the commanders of the Sabines to give battle at dawn, having sent for the army at Fidenae, Tarquinius, learning their intention — for the one carrying the letters from the commanders there to those yonder was captured — used the following stratagem against what had befallen from chance.

51.3. Dividing his force in two, he sent the one part by night, unobserved by the enemy, onto the road leading from Fidenae; the other, when bright day came, he drew up and led out of the camp as if for battle. And the Sabines, taking courage, came out against them, seeing the enemy not many and thinking their own force from Fidenae would presently be at hand. These, then, having taken their stand, fought, and the contest was for a long time equally balanced; but those sent forward beforehand by Tarquinius, turning back by night from the road and getting in the rear of the Sabines, came on.

51.4. The Sabines, seeing these and recognizing them by their arms and standards, lost their reckoning and, throwing away their arms, tried to save themselves. But safety was impossible for most, surrounded in a circle by enemies, and the Roman cavalry, pressing on, shut them off on every side; so that some few got out from under the danger, but the greater part were cut down by the enemy or surrendered themselves. Nor did those left at the camp hold out, but the rampart too was taken at the first assault; and there, along with the Sabines' own goods, all the Romans' property, with many captives still untouched, was recovered for those who had lost it.

52.1. When the first trial had gone according to his purpose, Tarquinius, taking up his force, came against the Sabines encamped at Fidenae, to whom the destruction of their own was not yet plain. They too chanced to have come forth beforehand from the camp and to be already on the road; and when they came near and saw fixed on spear-points the heads of their own commanders — for the Romans held them out to terrify the enemy — learning that their other army had been destroyed, they performed no further noble deed, but, turning to supplications and entreaties, surrendered themselves.

52.2. Both armies having been so shamefully and miserably swept away, the Sabines, shut up into narrow hopes, and fearing for their cities lest they be taken by assault, sent embassies concerning peace, surrendering themselves to be subject to Tarquinius and henceforth tributary. Having made a treaty with them and received the cities on the same terms, he went off to Suessa. Thence, taking up the force left there and the spoils and the other baggage, he returned to Rome, bringing back the army enriched.

52.3. After this also he made many incursions into the Volscian territory, sometimes with the whole force, sometimes with a part, and became master of much booty. And when most things were now going according to his mind, a war arose from his neighbours, both long in time — for it was waged for seven years continuously — and great by reason of grievous and unexpected sufferings. From what causes it began, and what end it had — since it was accomplished by treacherous deceit and an extraordinary stratagem — I will relate in a few words.

53.1. There was a city of the Latin race, a colony of the Albans, distant from Rome a hundred stadia, lying on the road that leads to Praeneste; they called it Gabii. It is now no longer wholly inhabited, except for those parts where there are inns along the road; but at that time it was as populous as any and large. One might conjecture its size and dignity from beholding the ruins of houses in many places and the circuit of its wall,

53.2. for most of it still stands. Into this city flowed together some of the Pometini who had escaped from Suessa when Tarquinius took their city, and many of the exiles from Rome; these, begging and importuning the Gabini to avenge them, and promising many gifts if they should return to their own, declaring the overthrow of the tyrant possible and easy, since those in the city too would join, persuaded them — the Volscians also having added their zeal, for they too sent embassies asking for alliance — to take up the war against Tarquinius.

53.3. After this there were invasions and incursions with great armies into one another's land, and battles, as was natural, sometimes few against few, sometimes all against all, in which often the Gabini, routing the Romans up to their walls and laying many low, plundered the country without fear; and often the Romans, pushing back the Gabini and shutting them into the city, carried off many slaves and much booty of theirs.

54.1. These things happening continually, both sides were compelled to fortify whatever was defensible in the country and to establish garrisons in them for the refuge of the farmers; from which, setting out, they destroyed the brigand-bands, and, if they saw any small part separated from a large army and, as is natural in foraging, undisciplined through contempt, descending in a body they destroyed it; and through fear of one another's sudden inroads they built up and fortified with ditches whatever of the cities was assailable and easy to take by ladders.

54.2. But Tarquinius was the more active about these things, and he strengthened with abundant labour the part of the city's circuit that faced the Gabini, digging a wider ditch and raising a higher wall and dividing the place with closer towers; for at this part especially the city seemed to be unfortified, being elsewhere fairly secure and hard of approach throughout the rest of its circuit.

54.3. And there was bound to befall — what is wont to happen to all cities in long wars, the land being ravaged by the continual inroads of the enemy and no longer bearing crops — a scarcity of all food in both, and terrible despondency about the future. But the lack of necessities pressed the Romans worse than the Gabini, and the poorest of them, suffering most, thought they ought to make agreements with the Gabini and conclude the war on whatever terms those should wish.

55.1. Tarquinius being distressed at what had happened, neither enduring to conclude the war shamefully nor able to hold out any longer, but contriving all manner of attempts and putting together every kind of guile, the eldest of his sons, Sextus by name, having communicated his plan to his father alone, and being thought to attempt a bold thing involving great danger, yet not impossible — his father consenting that he should do as he wished — feigns a quarrel with his father about the conclusion of the war;

55.2. and having been scourged by him with rods in the Forum and otherwise outraged, so that the matter became notorious, first he sent of his companions the most trustworthy as deserters to tell the Gabini secretly that he had resolved to make war on his father by going over to them, if he should receive pledges that they would protect him as they did the other exiles from Rome and would not give him up to his father, hoping to settle their own private enmities to their own

55.3. advantage. When the Gabini had gladly heard the proposal and agreed to do him no wrong, he came, bringing with him many companions and clients, as a deserter, and, that they might the more believe him to be telling the truth about his revolt from his father, bringing much silver and gold; and there flocked to him after this many of those from the city, pretending to flee the tyranny,

55.4. and there was now a strong band about him. The Gabini, thinking a great advantage had accrued to them, many having come over to them, and hoping that before long they would have Rome in their power, and still more deceived by what the deserter from his father did, going forth continually into the country and seizing much plunder — for his father, knowing beforehand to what places he would come, had provided abundant booty and the strongholds unguarded, and continually sent those who were to be destroyed by him, choosing from the citizens those whom he held in suspicion — from all these things thinking the man a faithful friend to them and a good general, and many of them too having been bribed by him with money, they bring him to the supreme command.

56.1. Having become master of so great an authority, Sextus, by deceit and trickery, sent secretly, unobserved by the Gabini, one of his servants to his father, both to declare the authority he had received and to learn

56.2. what he ought to do. Tarquinius, not wishing even the servant to know what he ordered his son to do, taking the messenger, came forth into the garden adjoining the palace. There chanced to be poppies growing in it, already full of seed and at the season of harvest; passing through these, with his staff he kept striking off the head of each poppy that overtopped the rest.

56.3. Having done this, he sent off the messenger without any answer to him who often asked — imitating, as it seems to me, the device of Thrasybulus the Milesian. For he too, when Periander the tyrant of the Corinthians once asked, through the messenger sent to him, how he might most securely hold the rule, sent no word in answer, but bidding the one who had come from him to follow, led him through a field sown with grain and, breaking off the ears that overtopped, threw them on the ground, teaching that one ought to lop off and destroy the most eminent of the citizens.

56.4. Tarquinius then having done much the like, Sextus, understanding his father's meaning — that he bade him do away with the most eminent of the Gabini — summoned the multitude into an assembly and, making a long speech about himself, that, having taken refuge in their faith together with his companions, he was in danger of being seized by certain men and given up to his father, was ready to lay down the command, and wished to depart from the city before suffering any terrible thing, weeping at the same time and bewailing his own fortune, like those who in truth are in agony for their lives.

57.1. When the multitude was roused and with great eagerness inquired who they were that meant to betray him, he named the most distinguished of the Gabini, Antistius Petro, who, having taken many earnest measures in peace and fulfilled many commands in war, had become the most distinguished of all; and when the man defended himself and, conscious of nothing, submitted to every examination, Sextus said he wished to search his house, sending others, and that he himself would remain in the assembly with the man until those sent should come.

57.2. For he had corrupted some of his servants with money, who had received the letters contrived for the destruction of Petro, sealed with his father's seal, and laid them away within. When those sent to the search — for Petro made no objection, but allowed his house to be searched — found where the letters were hidden, they came to the assembly bringing many other sealed letters and the one written to Antistius; and Sextus, saying he recognized his father's seal, broke it and, giving it to the secretary, ordered him to read it.

57.3. It was written therein that, best of all, his son should be given up to him alive and the agreed-upon rewards received, but, if this were impossible, that his head should be cut off and sent. And for him who should do this, and for those who shared in the deed, besides the other rewards he had earlier promised, he said he would give the citizenship at Rome and enrol them all in the number of the patricians, and bestow houses and allotments and

57.4. many other great gifts. At these things the Gabini, being enraged, kill Antistius — who was struck dumb at the unexpected calamity and could not even utter a voice for his misfortune — by pelting him with stones; and the search and punishment of the others who had planned the same things as Petro they entrusted to Sextus to carry out. He, entrusting the guarding of the gates to his own companions, that those under accusation might not escape him, sending to the houses of the most distinguished men, killed many of the Gabini, and good men.

58.1. While these things were being done, there being a tumult in the city as over so great an evil, Tarquinius, learning what was happening through letters, came up leading his force, and about the middle of the night, having got near the city, when the gates were opened by those prepared for the purpose, entered and without effort became master of the city.

58.2. When the calamity was known, all bewailing themselves as to what they would suffer, and expecting slaughters and enslavements and all the terrible things that befall those captured by tyrants — or, if they fared best, having condemned themselves to slavery and confiscation of goods and the like — Tarquinius did none of the things they expected and feared, although he was bitter in anger and inexorable in his punishments of enemies.

58.3. For he neither killed any of the Gabini nor expelled them from the city nor punished them with loss of citizen rights or confiscation of goods; but, summoning the multitude into an assembly and changing from a tyrannical to a kingly manner, he said he gave them back their own city and conceded to them the property they had, and along with these granted to all the equal citizenship of the Romans — not through goodwill toward the Gabini, but that, by doing this, he might hold the rule of the Romans more securely; thinking the strongest guard of himself and his children would be the faith of those who beyond hope had been saved and had recovered all their own.

58.4. And, that no fear about the future might remain to them, nor any doubt whether these things would remain firm for them, having written down on what just terms they should be friends, he completed the oaths concerning these matters in the assembly forthwith and swore over the victims. Of these oaths there is a memorial lying at Rome in the temple of Jupiter Pistius, whom the Romans call Sancus — a wooden shield covered with the hide of the ox sacrificed over the oaths at that time, inscribed in archaic letters with the agreements made by them. Having done these things and appointed his son Sextus king of the Gabini, he led off his force. The war against the Gabini, then, had such an end.

59.1. After this deed Tarquinius, giving the people rest from campaigns and wars, busied himself about the building of the temples, being eager to fulfil the vows of his grandfather. For that man, fighting in his last war against the Sabines, had vowed to Jupiter and Juno and Athena that, if he should prevail in the battle, he would build them temples; and the crag where the gods were to be established he had worked out with great substructures and mounds, as I said in the preceding Book, but had not lived to complete the building of the temples. This work, then, Tarquinius, choosing to accomplish from the tithe of the spoils from Suessa, set all the craftsmen at the labours.

59.2. Here, it is said, a certain marvellous prodigy underground occurred while the foundations were being dug and the digging had already gone to a great depth: there was found the head of a man newly slain, having the face like that of a living man, and the blood flowing down from the severing still warm and fresh.

59.3. Seeing this prodigy, Tarquinius ordered the workmen to stay the digging; and summoning the native diviners, he inquired of them what the prodigy meant to signify. When they made no declaration, but referred the knowledge of such things to the Tyrrhenians, inquiring of them and learning who was the most distinguished of the prodigy-interpreters among the Tyrrhenians, he sent to him the most reputable of the citizens as envoys.

60.1. When these men had come to the house of the prodigy-interpreter, they met a youth coming out, to whom, saying that they were envoys of the Romans wishing to meet the diviner, they asked him to announce it to him. And the young man said: "He whom you wish to meet is my father; he is busy at present, but it will be possible for you to go in to him after a little time.

60.2. And while you await him, declare to me on what business you have come. For it will be to your advantage, if you are about through inexperience to err in the question, to be taught by me to make no mistake; for no small part of the observations in divination is a right question." It seemed good to the men to do so, and they tell him the prodigy. And he, when he had heard it, after a short pause, said: "Hear, men of Rome; the prodigy my father will interpret for you, and will lie in nothing — for it is not lawful for a diviner; but as to what, in speaking and answering the questions, you may say and be free from error and falsehood — for it concerns you to have foreknown these things — learn from me.

60.3. When you have related the prodigy to him, saying that he does not exactly understand what you say, he will mark off with his staff a portion of the earth, some part or other; then he will say to you, 'This is the Tarpeian hill, and this part of it looks toward the east, this toward the west,

60.4. this northern part, and this opposite, southern.' Pointing these out with his staff, he will inquire of you in which of these parts the head was found. What, then, do I advise you to answer? Not to admit that the prodigy was found in any of these places which he, pointing with his staff, may inquire about, but to say that it was at Rome, among us, on the Tarpeian hill. If you keep these answers and are in no way led aside by him, recognizing that what is fated cannot be altered, he will interpret to you what the prodigy means to signify, and will not conceal it."

61.1. Having learned these things, the envoys, when the old man had leisure and someone came forth to fetch them, going in, tell the diviner the prodigy. And as he played the sophist, drawing on the earth circular lines and again other straight ones, and making concerning each place his questions about the finding, the envoys, untroubled in mind, kept the same answer, as the diviner's son had suggested to them, always naming Rome and the Tarpeian hill and asking the interpreter not to appropriate the sign, but to speak from

61.2. the best and the most just. Not being able to deceive the men nor to appropriate the omen, the diviner says to them: "Men of Rome, tell your fellow citizens that it is fated that this place, in which you found the head, should become the head of all Italy." From that time the hill is called Capitoline, after the head found in it; for the Romans call heads capita.

61.3. Hearing these things from the envoys, Tarquinius set the craftsmen to the works; and he wrought out most of the temple, but did not live to complete the whole work, being expelled from his rule sooner; rather it was in the third consulship that the city of the Romans brought it to completion. It was made standing upon a lofty foundation, eight hundred feet in circuit, having each side nearly two hundred feet; and one would find but a small difference of the excess of the length over the breadth, not a whole fifteen feet.

61.4. For upon the same foundations the temple built after the conflagration, in the time of our fathers, was found to differ from the ancient one only in the costliness of the material — being surrounded, on the front part that looks toward the south, with a triple row of columns, and on the sides with a single row. In it are three parallel chambers having common sides: the middle that of Jupiter, and on either side that of Juno and that of Athena, covered by one pediment and one roof.

62.1. There is told also another very marvellous piece of good fortune said to have belonged to the city of the Romans in the rule of Tarquinius, bestowed by the goodwill of some god or divinity; which not for a short time, but throughout the whole life of the city, has often saved it from great evils.

62.2. A certain woman, not of the country, came to the tyrant wishing to sell nine books full of Sibylline oracles. When Tarquinius did not think fit to buy the books at the price asked, she went away and burned three of them; and after no long time, bringing the remaining six, she offered them for sale at the same price. Being thought foolish and laughed at for asking the same price for the fewer that she could not get even for the more, she went away again and burned half of those that remained, and bringing the remaining

62.3. three, asked the same amount of gold. Marvelling at the woman's purpose, Tarquinius sent for the augurs and, relating the matter to them, asked what he ought to do. They, learning from certain signs that he had turned away a god-sent good, and declaring it a great misfortune that he had not bought all the books, bade him count out to the woman the gold she asked and take the oracles that remained.

62.4. The woman, then, having given the books and bidden him keep them carefully, vanished from among men; and Tarquinius, choosing two distinguished men of the citizens and joining to them two public slaves, committed to those men the guarding of the books. Of these, one, Marcus Atilius, thought to have done some wrong concerning the trust and being denounced by one of the public slaves, he sewed up in an oxhide, as a parricide, and cast into the sea.

62.5. After the expulsion of the kings the city, taking over the charge of the oracles, appoints the most distinguished men its guardians, who hold this care for life, being released from campaigns and from the other public business of the city; and it sets public slaves beside them, without whom it does not permit the men to make their inspections of the oracles. In short, the Romans guard nothing, neither holy nor sacred possession, so much as the Sibylline prophecies. They use them whenever the senate so votes, when sedition seizes the city, or some great misfortune befalls in war, or some prodigies and great apparitions, hard to interpret, appear to them, as has often happened. These oracles remained until the so-called Marsic War, lying underground in the temple of Capitoline Jupiter in a stone chest, guarded by ten men.

62.6. But after the third year past the hundred and seventieth Olympiad, the temple being burned — whether from a plot, as some think, or of itself — these too, along with the other offerings of the god, were destroyed by the fire. Those now existing are collected from many places, some brought from the cities in Italy, some from Erythrae in Asia, by decree of the senate three envoys being sent for the transcription; and others copied from other cities and from private men; among which are found some interpolated into the Sibylline oracles, and they are detected by the so-called acrostics; and I say what Terentius Varro has recorded in his treatise on theology.

63.1. Having accomplished these things in peace and in wars and having founded two colonies — the one called Signia not by deliberate purpose but of itself, the soldiers having wintered in the place and built the camp so that it differed in no way from a city; Circeii by deliberate reckoning, because it lay well, in relation to the Pomptine plain, the largest of those about Latium, and to the sea adjoining it; it is a peninsula-like crag, fairly high, lying on the Tyrrhenian sea, where the story is that Circe, the daughter of the Sun, dwelt — and having assigned both colonies to two of his sons as founders, Circeii to Arruns and Signia to Titus, having then no further fear concerning the rule, on account of the outrage to a woman, whom his eldest son Sextus violated, he is driven both from the rule and from the city, the divine power having foretold to him the calamity that was to come upon his house by many

63.2. other omens, and by this last. Eagles, coming together into the garden adjoining the palace in the season of spring, built a nest on the top of a lofty palm-tree. While these eagles had their young still unfledged, vultures, flying upon them in a body, scattered the nest and killed the young, and the eagles coming back from foraging they drove from the palm-tree, tearing and striking them with their talons.

63.3. Seeing these omens, and guarding himself, in case he might be able to ward off his fate, Tarquinius was not strong enough to overcome destiny; but, the patricians attacking him and the people uniting in mind, he was expelled from the rule. Who they were that began the uprising, and by what means they came to the deed, I will try to set forth in a few words.

64.1. Tarquinius was besieging the city of the Ardeates, making the pretext that they received the exiles from Rome and helped them concerning their return; but, as the truth was, plotting against it on account of its wealth, it being the most prosperous of the cities in Italy. The Ardeates fighting back nobly and the siege becoming long, both those at the camp, worn out by the prolongation of the war, and those in the city, exhausted by the contributions, were ready for revolt, if any beginning should be made.

64.2. At this very time Sextus, the eldest of the sons of Tarquinius, having been sent by his father to a city which was called Collatia to render certain military services, was lodged with a kinsman, Lucius Tarquinius

64.3. surnamed Collatinus. This man Fabius says was the son of Egerius, concerning whom I have shown before that he was the brother's son of Tarquinius the former king of the Romans, and, appointed governor of Collatia, was himself called Collatinus from his stay in that city and left the same surname to his descendants; but I am persuaded that this man too was the grandson of Egerius, if indeed he was of the same age as the sons of Tarquinius, as Fabius and the other historians have recorded; for the chronology confirms this supposition for me.

64.4. Collatinus, then, chanced to be at the camp at that time; but the wife who dwelt with him, a Roman, the daughter of Lucretius, a distinguished man, entertained him as a kinsman of her husband with much zeal and friendliness. This woman, the fairest and most virtuous of the women in Rome, Sextus attempted to corrupt, having earlier still restrained himself, whenever he was lodged with his kinsman, but then thinking he had a fitting occasion.

64.5. When after supper he had gone away to sleep, having waited through a great part of the night, when he thought all were asleep, rising he came to the chamber in which he knew Lucretia was sleeping, and, unobserved by those sleeping at the doors of the chamber, entered, holding a sword.

65.1. Standing over the bed — the woman being awakened at once with the sense of the noise and asking who it was — he told his name and bade her be silent and remain in the chamber, threatening to slay her if she should attempt to flee or cry out. Having terrified the woman in this way, he held out to her two choices, of which he asked her to choose which she preferred, death with

65.2. shame or life with happiness. "For if you consent," he said, "to gratify me, I will make you my wife, and you shall reign with me — now over the city which my father has given me, and after his death over the Romans and the Latins and the Tyrrhenians and all the others over whom he rules. For I know that I shall receive my father's kingship, as is just, being the eldest of his sons. And as for all the good things which kings have, of all which you shall be mistress with me, what need is there to teach you who know it well?

65.3. But if you attempt to resist, wishing to save your chastity, I will kill you, and, slaughtering one of the servants upon you, I will lay your bodies together and will say that, having caught you behaving shamefully with the slave, I punished you, avenging the outrage to my kinsman; so that your end will be shameful and reproachful, and your body will obtain neither burial nor any other of the customary rites."

65.4. As he was vehement, both threatening and entreating and swearing he spoke the truth in each of his sayings, Lucretia came into a constraint, fearing the dishonour about her death, to yield and to suffer him to accomplish what he wished.

66.1. When day came, he departed to the camp, having fulfilled a wicked and destructive desire; but Lucretia, bearing terribly what had happened, as quickly as she could, mounting her carriage, set off for Rome, clad in black raiment and hiding a small dagger beneath her robe, neither greeting any of those who met and saluted her, nor answering those who wished to learn what she had suffered, but thoughtful and downcast, with her eyes full of tears.

66.2. When she came into her father's house — there chanced to be some kinsmen present with him — taking hold of his knees and falling about him, for a time she wept, uttering no word; then, when her father raised her up and asked her to say what she had suffered, she said: "I become your suppliant, father, having endured a terrible and irremediable outrage; avenge me and do not overlook your own daughter,

66.3. who has suffered worse than death." When he marvelled, and all the others, and he asked her to say who had outraged her and what kind of outrage, she said: "You shall hear my calamities, father, before long; but grant me first this favour which I ask: summon as many friends and kinsmen as you can, that they may hear from me, who have suffered the terrible things, and not from others. And when you have learned the shameful and terrible constraints that seized me, take counsel with them how you will avenge me and yourself, and make not long the time between."

67.1. When, by a swift and earnest summons, the most distinguished men had come together into the house, as she asked, she tells them the whole matter, taking it up from the beginning. And after this, greeting her father and making many supplications both of him and of those present with him, and praying to the gods and divinities to grant her a swift release from life, she draws the dagger which she kept hidden beneath her robes, and, dealing a single blow through her breast, drives the sword as far as the heart.

67.2. An outcry and lamentation and beating of breasts of the women seizing the whole house, the father, throwing himself about the body, embraced and called upon her and tended her as if she would recover from the wound; but she, gasping in his arms and breathing out her life, dies. To the Romans present the calamity seemed so terrible and pitiable that with one voice they all cried out that it were ten thousand times better for them to die for freedom than to overlook such outrages committed by the tyrants.

67.3. There was among them a certain Publius Valerius, a descendant of one of the Sabines who came with Tatius to Rome, an active and prudent man. He is sent by them to the camp, both to tell the husband of Lucretia what had happened and, with him, to bring about the revolt of the soldiery from the tyrants.

67.4. Just as he had gone out of the gates, by divine providence Collatinus met him coming to the city from the camp, knowing nothing of the evils that had seized his house; and with him Lucius Junius, whose surname was Brutus — which, interpreted into the Greek tongue, would be "stupid"; concerning whom it is necessary to say a little beforehand, since the Romans declare him to have been the chief cause of the overthrow of the tyrants — who he was and from whom and why he obtained this surname which in no way belonged to him.

68.1. This man's father was Marcus Junius, a descendant of one of those who set out with Aeneas on the colony, numbered among the most distinguished of the Romans for valour; and his mother was Tarquinia, the daughter of the former king Tarquinius; and he himself shared in all the nurture and education of the country, and had a nature opposing nothing of the noble things.

68.2. But when Tarquinius, having killed Tullius along with many other good men, made away also with his father by a secret death, for no wrong, but led on to a desire for the wealth which he possessed from an ancient and ancestral prosperity, and with him his elder brother, who showed a noble spirit and would not have endured not to avenge his father's death — Brutus, being still young and utterly bereft of kindred help, undertook to do a thing most prudent of all, to falsely feign upon himself an assumed folly; and he continued all the time thereafter, until he thought he had the suitable occasion, keeping up the pretence of madness, from which he obtained this surname; and this saved him from suffering any terrible thing at the hands of the tyrant, while many good men were destroyed.

69.1. For Tarquinius, despising the folly which seemed to be about him but was not in truth, took away all his ancestral property, supplying him a little for his daily living, and, as an orphan child still needing guardians, kept him under himself and permitted him to live with his own sons — not through honour, as he pretended to those near him, as being a kinsman, but that he might furnish laughter to the youths, saying many foolish things and doing things like those who are truly foolish.

69.2. And indeed, when he sent two of his sons, Arruns and Titus, to consult the Delphic oracle concerning the plague — for a certain unaccustomed disease fell, in his reign, upon maidens and children, by which many bodies were destroyed, but most grievous and hard to cure for pregnant women, killing the mothers along with their infants in the birth — wishing to learn from the god both the cause of the disease and the remedy, he sent him too along with the youths, who begged it, that they might have one to mock and outrage.

69.3. When the young men had come to the oracle and received the responses concerning the things for which they were sent, having honoured the god with offerings and laughed much at Brutus, because he dedicated a wooden staff to Apollo — but he had bored it through entirely like a flute and put in a golden rod, no one knowing — after this they asked the god to whom it was fated to receive the rule of the Romans; and the god answered them, "To him who first kisses his mother."

69.4. The young men, then, ignorant of the meaning of the oracle, agreed with one another to kiss their mother at the same time, wishing to hold the kingship in common; but Brutus, understanding what the god meant to make plain, as soon as he set foot on Italy, stooping down kissed the earth, thinking this to be the mother of all men. Such, then, were the things that had befallen this man before.

70.1. At that time, when he heard Valerius relating the things that had befallen Lucretia and her death, raising his hands to heaven he said: "O Zeus and all you gods who watch over the life of men, has that moment now come for which I, waiting, kept up this pretence of life? Is it fated for the Romans to be delivered, by me and through me, from this unbearable tyranny?"

70.2. Having said this, he went in haste to the house together with Collatinus and Valerius. And when he entered, Collatinus, seeing Lucretia lying in the midst and her father lying about her, with a great groan and embracing the dead, kissed her and called upon her and conversed with her as with the living, being out of his mind through

70.3. the calamity. While he was lamenting much, and the father in turn, and the whole house was possessed with weeping and wailing, Brutus, looking at them, said: "You will have ten thousand occasions, Lucretius and Collatinus and all you who are kin to the woman, in which you may weep for her; but now let us consider how we shall avenge her;

70.4. for this the present occasion demands." It seemed he spoke reasonably, and, seating themselves apart and removing out of the way the throng of household servants and hired labourers, they took counsel what they ought to do. First Brutus, beginning to speak about himself — that the folly which seemed to the many to be his was not true but assumed, and telling the reasons for which he had endured this pretence — and being thought the most prudent of all men, after this persuaded them all, taking the same resolve, to drive Tarquinius and his sons from the city, delivering many alluring words to this end. And when he saw all of one mind, he said there was need not of words nor of promises, but of deeds, if any of the things needful were to come to pass; and he said that he himself would lead in these.

70.5. Having said this and taking the dagger with which the woman had killed herself, and going to her body — for it still lay in the open, a most piteous spectacle — he swore by Mars and the other gods to do all that he could for the overthrow of the rule of the Tarquinii, and neither himself to be reconciled to the tyrants nor to permit those who were reconciled, but to hold as an enemy the one who did not wish the same things, and even to the death to be the enemy of the tyranny and those who fought along with it. And if he should transgress the oath, he prayed that such an end of life might befall both him and his children as had befallen the woman.

71.1. Having said this, he called all the others too to the same oath; and they, no longer hesitating, rose up and, receiving the sword from one another, swore. The oaths having been taken, after this they immediately sought what should be the manner of the attempt. And Brutus suggests to them the following: "First, let us keep the gates under guard, that Tarquinius may perceive nothing of what is being said and done in the city against the tyranny, before the things on our side are made

71.2. ready. Then, bringing the body of the woman as it is, defiled with blood, into the Forum and setting it forth in the open, let us summon the people into an assembly. And when they have assembled and we see the Forum full, let Lucretius and Collatinus come forward and lament their own fortunes, relating all that has happened.

71.3. Then let each of the others, coming forward, accuse the tyranny and call the citizens to freedom. And it will be according to the prayer of all the Romans, if they see us, the patricians, beginning the work of freedom; for they have suffered many terrible things from the tyrant and need but a small impulse. And when we have got the multitude eager to overthrow the monarchy, let us give them a vote that Tarquinius shall no longer rule the Romans, and let us send the decree about these matters to those at the camp with speed.

71.4. For those bearing arms too, if they learn that all in the city is hostile to the tyrants, will become eager for the freedom of their country, being no longer held by gifts as before nor able to bear the outrages of the sons and flatterers of Tarquinius."

71.5. When he had said this, Valerius, taking up the speech, said: "In other respects, Junius, you seem to me to reckon rightly; but concerning the assembly I still wish to learn who shall be the one to summon it according to the laws and to give the vote to the curiae. For this is assigned to a magistrate to do; and none of us holds any magistracy." And he, taking him up, said: "I, Valerius;

71.6. for I am commander of the Celeres, and it is assigned to me by the laws to summon an assembly whenever I wish. The tyrant gave me this office, the greatest there is, as to a fool who would neither know its power nor, if I should know, would use it; and I will be the first to deliver the speech against the tyrant."
