72.1. When all heard this, they praised him and asked him to say the rest, as having begun from a fine and lawful premise. And he said: "Since it seems good to you to do these things thus, let us consider again what magistracy shall be the one to govern the city after the overthrow of the kings, and by what man it shall be appointed; and, before this, what shall be the order of the constitution which, on ridding ourselves of the tyrant, we shall establish. For it is better to have deliberated everything before attempting so great a deed, and to leave nothing unexamined or unplanned. Let each of you, then,

72.2. declare what he thinks about these matters." After this many speeches were made by many. To some it seemed best to establish again a royal constitution, reckoning up all the goods which all the former kings had done the city; to others, no longer to entrust public affairs to one ruler, recounting the tyrannical lawlessnesses which many others had used against their own citizens, and Tarquinius at the last, but to make the council of the senate master of all, as in many of the Greek cities;

72.3. and others preferred neither of these constitutions, but counselled to establish a democracy as at Athens, alleging the outrages and greeds of the few and the dissensions that arise of the lowly toward the eminent, and declaring equality before the law to be, for a free city, the safest and most fitting of constitutions.

73.1. The choice appearing to all difficult and hard to decide, on account of the evils attending each of the constitutions, last of all Brutus, taking up the speech, said: "I, Lucretius and Collatinus and all you present, good men and of good fathers, think we ought to establish no new constitution for the present; for the moment to which we have been brought by circumstances is brief, in which to reorder the constitution of a city is not easy; and the trial of the change, even if we chance to deliberate best concerning it, is perilous and not without danger. And it will be possible for us later, when we are rid of the tyranny, with more authority and at leisure to choose the better constitution instead of the worse, if indeed there be any better than that which Romulus and Pompilius and all the kings after them established and handed down to us, from which our city has continued great and prosperous and ruling over many men.

73.2. But the grievous things which are wont to attend monarchies, from which they pass over into tyrannical cruelty and on account of which all men dislike them, these I advise you to correct now, and to guard against, that they may not ever arise even hereafter.

73.3. And what are these? First, since the many look to the names of things, and from these either accept some of the harmful or shun some of the useful — among which monarchy too happens to be — I advise you to change the name of the constitution and no longer to call those who are to have the authority over all kings or monarchs, but to give them some more moderate and more humane appellation.

73.4. Then not to make the single opinion of all masters, but to entrust the royal rule to two men, as I learn the Lacedaemonians do for many generations now, and on account of this form of government to be the best-governed and most prosperous of all the Greeks; for they will be less insolent and oppressive, the authority being divided in two and each having the same strength; and mutual respect, and prevention of living according to pleasure, and emulation toward the reputation of virtue, would most arise for each from this rule of equal honour.

74.1. And of the insignia which have been assigned to the kings, being many, if any present grievous and envied sights to the many, some I think we ought to diminish, others to take away — I mean these sceptres and the golden crowns and the purple and gold-bordered robes, except at certain festival seasons and in the processions of triumphs, when they shall take them up for the honour of the gods; for it will grieve no one, if they be rare. But for the men an ivory chair, sitting on which they shall give judgment, and a white robe with a purple border, and the twelve axes preceding them in their goings-forth, we should leave.

74.2. Besides these, what I think will be the most useful of all that has been said and the chief cause of those who take over the rule not erring much: not to allow the same men to rule for life; for an undefined rule, giving no account of what is done, is grievous to all, and from it tyranny grows; but to confine the power of the office to a year's term, as is done among the Athenians.

74.3. For the same man ruling and being ruled in turn, and laying down the authority before his mind is corrupted, restrains self-willed natures and does not let characters become drunk with power. If we establish these things, it will be possible for us both to reap the goods of the royal constitution and to be rid of the evils attending it.

74.4. And that the name of the royal authority, being ancestral to us and having come into the city with auspicious omens, the gods ratifying it, may be preserved for the sake of religion, let there always be appointed a king of the sacred rites, who shall hold this honour for life, released from all warlike and political occupation, having this one work alone, like the king, the leadership of the sacrifices, and nothing else.

75.1. In what manner each of these things shall be, hear from me. I will summon the assembly, as I said, since it is permitted me by law, and I will introduce a motion: that Tarquinius, together with his sons and his wife, be banished, debarred from the city and territory of the Romans for all time, and the offspring sprung from them. And when the citizens have voted the motion, declaring to them the constitution we intend to establish, I will choose an interrex who shall appoint those who are to take over public affairs; and I myself will lay down the office of the Celeres.

75.2. And the interrex appointed by me, convening the centuriate assembly, shall name those who are to hold the annual leadership and shall give the citizens a vote concerning them. And if it seems good to the majority of the centuries that the choice of the men be valid, and the auspices concerning them be fair, these men, taking over the axes and the rest of the symbols of royal authority, shall act so that we may dwell with a free country and that the Tarquinii may no longer have a return to it; for they will attempt, know it well, by persuasion and force and guile and every other means, to come back again to the rule, unless we guard against them.

75.3. These, then, are the greatest and most important of the things I have to say and advise you at present; but the particulars, being many and not easy now to examine with precision — for we have been gathered for a sharp moment — I think we ought to leave to the very men who shall take over the rule.

75.4. I say, however, that the men ought to consider everything with the council of the senate, as the kings did, and to do nothing apart from you, and to bring the resolutions of the senate to the people, as it was the custom of our ancestors to do, taking from it none of the things of which it was master in former times. For thus will their rule be most secure and most honourable."

76.1. When Junius Brutus had declared this opinion, all praised it, and at once, deliberating about the men who should take over the leadership, they judged that Spurius Lucretius, the father of her who had killed herself, should be appointed interrex; and that by him those who should have the authority of the kings should be named, Lucius Junius Brutus and Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus.

76.2. These magistrates they ordained should be called in their own tongue consuls; this name, interpreted into the Greek tongue, can mean "counsellors" or "foredeliberators," for the Romans call counsels consilia; but in course of time they were named by the Greeks hypatoi ("supreme"), from the greatness of their authority, because they rule over all and hold the highest place. For the ancients called the surpassing and

76.3. highest hypaton. Having deliberated and established these things, and having besought the gods with prayers to aid them as they reached after holy and just deeds, they went out into the Forum. And there followed them the servants carrying upon a bier spread with black coverings the corpse, untended and defiled with blood; and ordering it to be set before the senate-house, lofty and conspicuous, they summoned the people into an assembly.

76.4. When a crowd had gathered, not only of that then in the Forum but also of that throughout the whole city — for the heralds went through the lanes summoning the people to the Forum — Brutus, mounting the place where it was the custom for those summoning the assemblies to harangue, and stationing the patricians beside him, spoke as follows.

77.1. "Being about to make speeches to you, fellow citizens, concerning necessary and common affairs, I wish first to say a few things beforehand about myself. For to some of you, or rather, I know well, to many, I shall seem disturbed in mind, a man not in his right senses attempting to speak about the greatest things, who, being unsound, has need of guardians.

77.2. Know, then, that the common supposition which you all had about me as a fool was false and was contrived by no other but myself. And what compelled me to live neither as nature thought fit nor as befitted me, but as it was Tarquinius's wish and seemed likely to profit me, was fear for my life.

77.3. For Tarquinius, having killed my father at the same time as he took over the rule, that he might seize his property, which was very great, and having made away by a secret death with my elder brother, who would have avenged his father's death if he were not put out of the way, was not plainly going to spare me either, left bereft of my nearest kin, had I not feigned the assumed folly.

77.4. This fiction, being believed by the tyrant, saved me from suffering the same things as they, and has preserved me to the present time; but now for the first time — for the moment has come which I prayed for and awaited — having kept it for this five-and-twentieth year, I lay it aside. So much concerning myself.

78.1. The common affairs, for which I summoned you into the assembly, are these. Tarquinius — who got the rule neither according to our ancestral customs and laws, nor, since he got it, however he got it, used it well and in kingly fashion, but has surpassed in outrage and lawlessness all the tyrants that ever existed anywhere — him we, the patricians, meeting together, have resolved to deprive of his authority, a thing that ought to have been done long ago, but which we now do at a fitting moment; and we have summoned you, plebeians, that, declaring our own purpose, we may ask you to become our fellow combatants in working freedom for our country — freedom which neither was it possible for us to share before, ever since Tarquinius held the rule, nor will it be possible hereafter, if we now grow soft.

78.2. If, then, I had as much time as I wished, or were about to speak to men ignorant, I would recount all the lawlessnesses of the tyrant, for which he would justly deserve to perish, not once, but many times, in the eyes of all; but since the moment that circumstances give me is brief, in which there is need to say little but to do much, and the words are addressed to men who know, I will remind you of the greatest and most manifest of his deeds, those that can obtain no defence whatever.

79.1. This is, fellow citizens, that Tarquinius who, before taking over the rule, made away by poison with Arruns his legitimate brother, because he was unwilling to be wicked, having taken as helper in this abomination that brother's wife, the sister of his own consort, whom this enemy of the gods had long been corrupting;

79.2. this is the man who, in the same days and by the same poisons, killed his wedded wife, a modest woman who had become a partner of children with him; and who did not even think fit to clear himself of the calumnies of both poisonings, as though they had not been done by himself, by using a piteous guise and a small pretence of mourning, but, immediately upon doing these marvellous deeds, before the pyres that received the wretched bodies had died down, feasted his friends and celebrated nuptials and led the murderess bride to the chamber of her sister, confirming with her his secret agreements — being the first and only to introduce into the city of the Romans impious and accursed deeds done nowhere in the land of Greek or

79.3. barbarian. And what things, plebeians, did he work — the notorious and terrible attempts upon both his fathers-in-law, who were already at the setting of their life? Servius Tullius, the most equitable of kings and the one who did you the most good, he openly slaughtered and did not permit his body to obtain a proper carrying-out or burial;

79.4. and Tarquinia, that man's wife, whom it befitted him to honour as a mother, being his father's sister and zealous on his behalf, before she had mourned and done the customary rites for her husband who was beneath the earth, the wretched woman he made away with by the noose — those by whom he was saved and among whom he was reared and whom he was about to succeed after their death, had he waited a little, until the natural death came to them.

80.1. But why do I find fault with these things, having so many of his lawlessnesses to accuse, apart from those done to his kinsmen and fathers-in-law — those accomplished against the country and all of us, if indeed one must call them lawlessnesses and not overthrows and abolitions of all the customs and usages? To begin with the leadership, that I may start from this, how did he take it over? Was it as the kings before him? Whence?

80.2. Far from it. Those, indeed, were all brought to power by you according to ancestral customs and laws: first, a decree being written by the senate, to which is assigned the preliminary deliberation about all public matters; then interreges being chosen, to whom the council entrusts to decide, from those worthy of the rule, the most fit; after this, the people casting a vote in the elections, with which the law wishes all the greatest matters to be ratified; and upon all these, the auspices and victims and the other signs being favourable, without which there would be no benefit of human zeal and forethought.

80.3. Come, then, which of these does any of you know to have occurred when Tarquinius took the rule? What preliminary decree of the council? What decision of interreges? What voting of the people? What favourable auspices? I do not say, though I ought, that, if indeed it was to be well, none of the customary things according to the laws should have been omitted; but if anyone can show even one only of these to have occurred, I do not think fit to slander those omitted. How, then, did he come to power? By arms and force and conspiracies of wicked men, as is the custom of tyrants, against your will and to your displeasure.

80.4. Come, then — but since he held the rule, however he got it, has he used it in kingly fashion, emulating the former rulers, who continued saying and doing such things as made the city more prosperous and greater for those who came after than they received it? And who, being of sound mind, would say this, seeing how piteously and badly we have all been treated by him?

81.1. Our own calamities, then — those of the patricians — at which even one of our enemies, learning them, would weep, I pass over in silence: that few of many are we left, that from great we have become lowly, that we have come to poverty and terrible want, having fallen from many blessed goods. Those brilliant and powerful and great men, through whom our city was once illustrious, some have perished,

81.2. others are exiles from their country. But your affairs, plebeians, how stand they? Has he not taken from you your laws, taken from you your gatherings for sacred rites and sacrifices, stopped those who held elections and voted and assembled about public matters, and compelled you to toil at things deserving shame, like bought slaves — quarrying, cutting timber, bearing burdens, consumed in pits and abysses, getting not the smallest respite from your evils?

81.3. What, then, will be the limit of our calamities, and for how long a time, suffering these things, shall we endure, and when shall we recover our ancestral freedom? When Tarquinius dies? By Zeus! And what more shall we have then — what not worse? For we shall have three Tarquinii instead of one,

81.4. far more polluted than the father. For where the one who became a tyrant from a private man, and late began to be wicked, perfects all tyrannical wickedness, of what sort must we think those sprung from him will be, whose race is wicked, whose nurture wicked, and who never had occasion either to see or to learn anything political and moderate being done? And that you may not conjecture their accursed natures but learn them exactly — what kind of whelps the tyranny of Tarquinius rears up for you — behold the deed of one of them, the eldest.

82.1. This is the daughter of Spurius Lucretius, whom the tyrant appointed prefect of the city when he went out to the war, and the wife of Tarquinius Collatinus, the kinsman of the tyrants and one who suffered much hardship on their behalf. This woman, wishing to be chaste and loving her own husband, as befits a good wife, when Sextus was lodged with her on account of the kinship the past night, Collatinus being then absent at the camp, was unable to escape the licentious outrage of the tyranny, but, like a captive overpowered by necessity, endured to suffer what is not lawful for a free woman to suffer.

82.2. Indignant at this and deeming the outrage unbearable, when she had recounted to her father and the other kinsmen the constraints that seized her, having made many entreaties and curses that they should become avengers of her evils, and having drawn the sword hidden beneath her bosom, before her father's eyes, plebeians, she dyed the iron through her own entrails.

82.3. O wondrous woman, and worthy of many praises for your noble resolve — you are gone and perished, not having endured tyrannical outrage, disdaining all the pleasures in living, that no such thing might befall you to suffer again. Then you, Lucretia, having got a woman's nature, had the spirit of a noble man; but shall we, being men, prove worse than women in virtue? And to you, because you were tyrannized over for a single night and robbed by force of your unstained honour, death seemed sweeter and more blessed than life; but shall not this same thought come to us, from whom Tarquinius, tyrannizing now not one day but the five-and-twentieth year, has taken away all the pleasures in living, having taken away freedom?

82.4. It is not, plebeians, to be endured by us, wallowing in such evils, being the descendants of those men who thought fit to ordain justice for others and undertook many dangers for rule and glory; but one of two things must be chosen by all, either a free life or a glorious death.

82.5. And the moment has come, such as we pray for: Tarquinius having departed from the city, the patricians leading the attempt, and nothing being lacking to us, if with zeal we proceed to the work — neither men, nor money, nor arms, nor generals, nor the rest of the equipment for war; for the city is full of all these. And it is shameful to think fit to rule the Volscians and the Sabines and ten thousand others, but ourselves to endure being slaves to others; and concerning the greed of Tarquinius to take up many wars, but concerning our own freedom, none.

83.1. By what resources, then, shall we proceed to the work, and by what alliances? For this remains to be said. First, by the hopes from the gods, whose sacred rites and precincts and altars Tarquinius pollutes with his blood-stained hands, full of every kindred abomination, when he begins sacrifices and libations; then by those from ourselves, who are neither few nor inexperienced in war; and besides these, by the aid from the allies, who, if we do not call them, will not think fit to meddle, but, if they see us laying claim to virtue, will gladly join in the war; for tyranny is hateful to all who wish to be free.

83.2. But if any of you fear the citizens at the camp with Tarquinius, as ones who will fight along with him and make war on us, they fear wrongly. For to them too the tyranny is grievous, and innate in all men is the longing for freedom, and every pretext for change is sufficient for those who toil by necessity; whom, if you shall vote to aid the country, neither fear will hold among the tyrants, nor favour, nor any other of the things that force or persuade men to do what is

83.3. not just. And if in any of them, through evil nature or wicked nurture, the love of tyranny is innate — not many, by Zeus — these too we will yoke with great necessities, so as to become from wicked, good; for we have as hostages in the city their children and wives and parents, which are more precious to each than his own life. These things, then, we will promise to restore to them, if they desert the tyrants, and, voting them immunity for what they have erred, we shall easily persuade them.

83.4. Therefore, with confidence, plebeians, and having good hopes for the future, go to the contest, about to undertake the fairest of all the wars you have ever loved. We, then — O ancestral gods, good guardians of this land, and divinities who have been allotted our fathers, and city most beloved of gods among cities, in which we obtained our birth and nurture — will defend you with counsels and words and hands and lives, and are ready to suffer all, whatever the divine power and necessity may bring.
83.5. And I divine that upon fair attempts a fortunate end will follow. May it be that all, taking the same courage and using one mind, both save us and be saved by us."

84.1. While Brutus was thus haranguing, continuous shouts at each of his statements arose from the multitude, signifying their will and their encouragement, and to most of them tears of pleasure flowed as they heard the marvellous and unexpected words; and various emotions, in no way like one another, seized the soul of each: griefs were mingled with pleasures, the former at the terrible things that had gone before, the latter at the goods expected; and angers fell out along with fears, the angers urging them to disdain safety for the working of evil upon the things they hated, the fears, by the reckoning that the overthrow of the tyranny would not be easy, bringing hesitation to their resolves.

84.2. When he ceased speaking, as if from one mouth all cried out the same cry, to lead them to arms. And Brutus, pleased, said: "Provided that you first, having learned the resolutions of the council, ratify what has been decreed. For it has been decreed by us that the Tarquinii be banished from the city of the Romans and from all the country over which the Romans rule, and all the race sprung from them; and that it be lawful for no one either to do or to say anything about the return of the Tarquinii; and if anyone be found acting contrary to this, that he die.

84.3. If it is your wish that this resolution be valid, dividing yourselves by curiae, cast your vote, and let this be the first beginning of the right of freedom for you." This was done; and when all the curiae had voted the banishment of the tyrants, Brutus, coming forward again, said: "Since the first things have been ratified by us as was needful, hear also the rest

84.4. of what we have deliberated concerning the constitution. To us, considering what magistracy shall be master of public affairs, it no longer seems good to establish a kingship, but to appoint two magistrates each year, who shall have royal authority, whom you shall appoint in the elections by casting your vote according to centuries. If, then, this too is your wish, ratify it by your vote." The people praised this opinion too, and there was no vote against it.

84.5. After this Brutus, coming forward, appoints as interrex, to take charge of the elections according to the ancestral laws, Spurius Lucretius; and he, dismissing the assembly, ordered all to come to the plain where it was their custom to hold the elections, bearing their arms, with speed. When they had come, he chooses two men to do all that the kings were permitted to do, Brutus and Collatinus; and the people, called by centuries, ratified the rule for the men. Such, then, were the things done in the city at that time.

85.1. King Tarquinius, when he heard from the messengers from the city — who were the first to escape before the gates were shut, reporting only this much, that Brutus held the assembly, demagoguing and calling the citizens to freedom — telling none of the others, hastened, taking up his sons and the most trustworthy of his companions, driving his horses at full rein, to forestall the revolt. But finding the gates shut and the battlements full of arms, he went off again to the camp as fast as he could, groaning and grievously suffering.

85.2. But it chanced that affairs there too were already ruined. For the consuls, foreseeing his swift arrival at the city, send letters by other roads to those at the camp, calling on them to revolt from the tyrant and making plain the resolutions of those in the town.

85.3. These letters the prefects left by the king, Titus Herminius and Marcus Horatius, having received, read in the assembly; and asking opinions according to centuries what they ought to do, since it seemed good to all to hold valid the things judged by the city, they no longer received Tarquinius when he arrived.

85.4. Thrust away from this hope too, the king flees with a few to the city of the Gabini, of which he had appointed king the elder of his sons, Sextus, as I said before — being now grey in age, but having held the kingship twenty-five years. And Herminius and Horatius, having established a truce of the war with the Ardeates for fifteen years, led off the forces homeward. The royal constitution, then, having lasted, after the founding of Rome, two hundred and forty-four years in number, and having, under the last king, become a tyranny, was, for these causes and by these men, dissolved.
